Lagrange Inversion

Ira M. Gessel∗ Address: Department of Mathematics
Brandeis University
Waltham, MA 02453-2700 Email address: gessel@brandeis.edu
Abstract.

We give a survey of the Lagrange inversion formula, including different versions and proofs, with applications to combinatorial and formal power series identities.

1. Introduction

The Lagrange inversion formula is one of the fundamental formulas of combinatorics. In its simplest form it gives a formula for the power series coefficients of the solution f⁡(x)f(x) of the function equation f⁡(x)=x​G​(f⁡(x))f(x)=xG(f(x)) in terms of coefficients of powers of GG. Functional equations of this form often arise in combinatorics, and our interest is in these applications rather than in other areas of mathematics.

There are many generalizations of Lagrange inversion: multivariable forms [28], qq-analogues [22, 23, 25, 71] noncommutative versions [6, 7, 23, 56] and others [29, 43, 45]. In this paper we discuss only ordinary one-variable Lagrange inversion, but in greater detail than elsewhere in the literature.

In section 2 we give a thorough discussion of some of the many different forms of Lagrange inversion, prove that they are equivalent to each other, and work through some simple examples involving Catalan and ballot numbers. We address a number of subtle issues that are overlooked in most accounts of Lagrange inversion (and which some readers may want to skip). In sections 3 we describe applications of Lagrange inversion to identities involving binomial coefficients, Catalan numbers, and their generalizations. In section 4, we give several proofs of Lagrange inversion, some of which are combinatorial.

A number of exercises giving additional results are included.

An excellent introduction to Lagrange inversion can be found in Chapter 5 of Stanley’s Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 2. Other expository accounts of Lagrange inversion can be found in Hofbauer [35], Bergeron, Labelle, and Leroux [5, Chapter 3], Sokal [68], and Merlini, Sprugnoli, and Verri [51].

1.1. Formal power series

Although Lagrange inversion is often presented as a theorem of analysis (see, e.g., Whittaker and Watson [76, pp. 132–133]), we will work only with formal power series and formal Laurent series. A good account of formal power series can be found in Niven [55]; we sketch here some of the basic facts. Given a coefficient ring CC, which for us will always be an integral domain containing the rational numbers, the ring C⁡[[x]]C[[x]] of formal power series in the variable xx with coefficients in CC is the set of all “formal sums” ∑n=0∞cn​xn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_{n}x^{n}, where cn∈Cc_{n}\in C, with termwise addition and multiplication defined as one would expect using distributivity: ∑n=0∞an​xn⋅∑n=0∞bn​xn=∑n=0∞cn​xn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}x^{n}\cdot\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}b_{n}x^{n}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_{n}x^{n}, where cn=∑i=0nai​bn−ic_{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}b_{n-i}. Differentiation of formal power series is also defined termwise. A series ∑n=0∞cn​xn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_{n}x^{n} has a multiplicative inverse if and only if c0c_{0} is invertible in CC. We may also consider the ring of formal Laurent series C⁡((x))C((x)) whose elements are formal sums ∑n=n0∞cn​xn\sum_{n=n_{0}}^{\infty}c_{n}x^{n} for some integer n0n_{0}, i.e., formal sums ∑n=−∞∞cn​xn\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}c_{n}x^{n} in which only finitely many negative powers of xx have nonzero coefficients. Henceforth will omit the word “formal” and speak of power series and Laurent series.

We can iterate the power series and Laurent series ring constructions, obtaining, for example the ring C​((x))​[[y]]C((x))[[y]] of power series in yy whose coefficients are Laurent series in xx. In any (possibly iterated) power series or Laurent series ring we will say that a set {fα}\{f_{\alpha}\} of series is summable if for any monomial mm in the variables, the coefficient of mm is nonzero in only finitely many fαf_{\alpha}. In this case the sum ∑αf\sum_{\alpha}f is well-defined and we will say that ∑αfα\sum_{\alpha}f_{\alpha} is summable. If we write ∑αfα\sum_{\alpha}f_{\alpha} as an iterated sum, then the order of summation is irrelevant. If f⁡(x)=∑ncn​xnf(x)=\sum_{n}c_{n}x^{n} is a Laurent series in C⁡((x))C((x)) and u∈Cu\in C, where CC may be a power series or Laurent series ring, then we say that that the substitution of uu for xx is admissible if f⁡(u)=∑ncn​unf(u)=\sum_{n}c_{n}u^{n} is summable, and similarly for multivariable substitutions. Admissible substitutions are homomorphisms. If uu is a power series or Laurent series g⁡(x)g(x) then f⁡(g⁡(x))f(g(x)), if summable, is called the composition of ff and gg. If f⁡(x)=c1​x+c2​x2+⋯f(x)=c_{1}x+c_{2}x^{2}+\cdots, where c1c_{1} is invertible in CC, then there is a unique power series g⁡(x)=c1−1​x+⋯g(x)=c_{1}^{-1}x+\cdots such that f⁡(g⁡(x))=xf(g(x))=x; this implies that g⁡(f⁡(x))=xg(f(x))=x. We call g⁡(x)g(x) the compositional inverse of f⁡(x)f(x) and write g⁡(x)=f​(x)⟨−1⟩g(x)=f(x)^{\langle-1\rangle}. For simplicity, we will always assume that if f⁡(x)=c1​x+c2​x2+⋯f(x)=c_{1}x+c_{2}x^{2}+\cdots, where c1≠0c_{1}\neq 0 then c1c_{1} is invertible. (Since CC is an integral domain, we can always adjoin c1−1c_{1}^{-1} to CC if necessary.)

The iterated power series rings C​[[x]]​[[y]]C[[x]][[y]] and C​[[y]]​[[x]]C[[y]][[x]] are essentially the same, in that both consist of all sums ∑m,n≥0cm,n​xm​yn\sum_{m,n\geq 0}c_{m,n}x^{m}y^{n}. We may therefore write C⁡[[x,y]]C[[x,y]] for either of these rings. However, the iterated Laurent series rings C​((x))​[[y]]C((x))[[y]], C​((y))​[[x]]C((y))[[x]], and C​[[y]]​((x))C[[y]]((x)) are all different: in the first we have (x−y)−1=∑n=0∞yn/xn+1(x-y)^{-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}y^{n}\!/x^{n+1}, in the second we have (x−y)−1=−∑n=0∞xn/yn+1(x-y)^{-1}=-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^{n}\!/y^{n+1}, and in the third x−yx-y is not invertible.

It is sometimes convenient to work with power series in infinitely many variables; for example, we may consider the power series ∑n=0∞rn​tn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r_{n}t^{n} where the rnr_{n} are independent indeterminates. Although we don’t give a formal definition of these series, they behave, in our applications, exactly as expected.

We use the notation [xn]⁡f⁡(x)\mathop{[x^{n}]}f(x) to denote the coefficient of xnx^{n} in the Laurent series f⁡(x)f(x). An important fact about the coefficient operator that we will use often, without comment, is that [xn]⁡xk​f​(x)=[xn−k]⁡f⁡(x)\mathop{[x^{n}]}x^{k}f(x)=\mathop{[x^{n-k}]}f(x).

The binomial coefficient (ak)\binom{a}{k} is defined to be a(a−1)⋯(a−k+1)/k!a(a-1)\cdots(a-k+1)/k! if kk is a nonnegative integer and 0 otherwise. Thus the binomial theorem (1+x)a=∑k=0∞(ak)​xk(1+x)^{a}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{a}{k}x^{k} holds for all aa.

2. The Lagrange inversion formula

2.1. Forms of Lagrange inversion

We will give several proofs of the Lagrange inversion formula in section 4. Here we state several different forms of Lagrange inversion and show that they are equivalent.

Theorem 2.1.1.

Let R⁡(t)R(t) be a power series not involving xx. Then there is a unique power series f=f⁡(x)f=f(x) such that f⁡(x)=x​R​(f⁡(x))f(x)=xR(f(x)), and for any Laurent series ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) and ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) not involving xx and any integer nn we have

[xn]⁡ϕ⁡(f)=1n​[tn−1]⁡ϕ′​(t)​R​(t)n,where ​n≠0,\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}\phi(f)=\frac{1}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-1}]}\phi^{\prime}(t)R(t)^{n},\ \text{where }n\neq 0, (2.1.1)
[xn]⁡ϕ⁡(f)=[tn]⁡(1−t​R′​(t)/R⁡(t))​ϕ​(t)​R​(t)n,\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}\phi(f)=\mathop{[t^{n}]}\bigl(1-tR^{\prime}(t)/R(t)\bigr)\phi(t)R(t)^{n}, (2.1.2)
ϕ⁡(f)=∑nxn​[tn]⁡(1−x​R′​(t))​ϕ​(t)​R​(t)n,\displaystyle\phi(f)=\sum_{n}x^{n}\mathop{[t^{n}]}(1-xR^{\prime}(t))\phi(t)R(t)^{n}, (2.1.3)
[xn]⁡ψ⁡(f)1−x​R′​(f)=[tn]⁡ψ⁡(t)​R​(t)n,\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}\frac{\psi(f)}{1-xR^{\prime}(f)}=\mathop{[t^{n}]}{\psi(t)R(t)^{n}}, (2.1.4)
[xn]⁡ψ⁡(f)1−f​R′​(f)/R⁡(f)=[tn]⁡ψ⁡(t)​R​(t)n.\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}\frac{\psi(f)}{1-fR^{\prime}(f)/R(f)}=\mathop{[t^{n}]}{\psi(t)R(t)^{n}}. (2.1.5)

We show here these formulas are equivalent in the sense that any one of them is easily derivable from any other; proofs of these formulas are given in section 4. It is clear that (2.1.4) and (2.1.5) are equivalent since x=f/R⁡(f)x=f/R(f). Taking ψ⁡(t)=(1−t​R′​(t)/R⁡(t))​ϕ​(t)\psi(t)=(1-tR^{\prime}(t)/R(t))\phi(t) shows that (2.1.2) and (2.1.5) are equivalent.

To derive (2.1.3) from (2.1.4), we rewrite (2.1.4) as

ψ⁡(f)1−x​R′​(f)=∑nxn​[tn]⁡ψ⁡(t)​R​(t)n.\frac{\psi(f)}{1-xR^{\prime}(f)}=\sum_{n}x^{n}\mathop{[t^{n}]}{\psi(t)R(t)^{n}}. (2.1.6)

Until now, we have assumed that ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) and ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) do not involve xx. We leave it to the reader to see that in (2.1.6) this assumption can be removed. Then (2.1.3) follows from (2.1.6) by setting ψ⁡(t)=(1−x​R′​(t))​ϕ​(t)\psi(t)=(1-xR^{\prime}(t))\phi(t), and similarly (2.1.6) follows from (2.1.3).

Although we allow RR to be an arbitrary power series in Theorem 2.1.1, if RR has constant term 0 then f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0, so we may assume now that RR has a nonzero constant term, and thus ff and R⁡(f)R(f) are nonzero. Then the equation f⁡(x)=x​R​(f⁡(x))f(x)=xR(f(x)) may be rewritten as f/R⁡(f)=xf/R(f)=x. So if we set g⁡(t)=t/R⁡(t)g(t)=t/R(t) then we have g⁡(f)=xg(f)=x, and thus g=f⟨−1⟩g=f^{\langle-1\rangle}. It is sometimes convenient to rewrite the formulas of Theorem 2.1.1 using gg, rather than RR. Since 1−t​R′​(t)/R⁡(t)=t​g′​(t)/g⁡(t)1-tR^{\prime}(t)/R(t)=tg^{\prime}(t)/g(t), formula (2.1.2) takes on a slightly simpler form (which will be useful later on) when expressed in terms of gg rather than RR:

[xn]⁡ϕ⁡(f)=[tn−1]⁡ϕ⁡(t)​g′​(t)g⁡(t)​(tg⁡(t))n=[t−1]⁡ϕ⁡(t)​g′​(t)g​(t)n+1,\mathop{[x^{n}]}\phi(f)=\mathop{[t^{n-1}]}\phi(t)\frac{g^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)}\left(\frac{t}{g(t)}\right)^{n}=\mathop{[t^{-1}]}\frac{\phi(t)g^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)^{n+1}}, (2.1.7)

For future use, we note also the corresponding form for (2.1.5):

[xn−1]⁡ψ⁡(f)f​g′​(f)=[tn]⁡ψ⁡(t)​(tg⁡(t))n=[t0]⁡ψ⁡(t)g​(t)n.\mathop{[x^{n-1}]}\frac{\psi(f)}{fg^{\prime}(f)}=\mathop{[t^{n}]}\psi(t)\left(\frac{t}{g(t)}\right)^{n}=\mathop{[t^{0}]}\frac{\psi(t)}{g(t)^{n}}. (2.1.8)

To show that (2.1.1) and (2.1.2) are equivalent, using (2.1.7) in place of (2.1.2), we show that

[t−1]⁡ϕ′​(t)g​(t)n=n​[t−1]⁡ϕ⁡(t)​g′​(t)g​(t)n+1\mathop{[t^{-1}]}\frac{\phi^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)^{n}}=n\mathop{[t^{-1}]}\frac{\phi(t)g^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)^{n+1}} (2.1.9)

But

ϕ′​(t)g​(t)n−n​ϕ⁡(t)​g′​(t)g​(t)n+1=dd​t​ϕ⁡(t)g​(t)n,\frac{\phi^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)^{n}}-n\frac{\phi(t)g^{\prime}(t)}{g(t)^{n+1}}=\frac{d\ }{dt}\frac{\phi(t)}{g(t)^{n}},

and the coefficient of t−1t^{-1} in the derivative of any Laurent series is 0, so (2.1.9) follows. This shows that (2.1.1) and (2.1.2) are equivalent if n≠0n\neq 0. If ϕ\phi is a power series, then the coefficient of x0x^{0} in ϕ⁡(f)\phi(f) is simply the constant term in ϕ\phi, but if ϕ\phi is a more general Laurent series, then the constant term in ϕ⁡(f)\phi(f) is not so obvious, and cannot be determined by (2.1.1). In equation (2.2.8) we will give a formula for the constant term in ϕ⁡(f)\phi(f) for all ϕ\phi.

The case ϕ⁡(t)=tk\phi(t)=t^{k} of (2.1.1), with R⁡(t)=t/g⁡(t)R(t)=t/g(t) may be written

[xn]⁡fk=kn​[tn−k]⁡(tg⁡(t))n=kn​[t−k]⁡g​(t)−n.\mathop{[x^{n}]}f^{k}=\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}\left(\frac{t}{g(t)}\right)^{n}=\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{-k}]}g(t)^{-n}. (2.1.10)

In other words, if g=f⟨−1⟩g=f^{\langle-1\rangle}, and for all integers kk, fk=∑nan,k​xnf^{k}=\sum_{n}a_{n,k}x^{n} and gk=∑nbn,k​xng^{k}=\sum_{n}b_{n,k}x^{n} then

an,k=kn​b−k,−na_{n,k}=\frac{k}{n}b_{-k,-n} (2.1.11)

for n≠0n\neq 0. Equation (2.1.11) is known as the Schur-Jabotinsky theorem. (See Schur [66, equation (10)] and Jabotinsky [37, Theorem II].)

2.2. Polynomials

We now give a slightly more general form of Lagrange inversion based on the fact that if two polynomials agree at infinitely many values than they are identically equal. This will imply that to prove our Lagrange formulas for all nn, it is sufficient to prove them in the case in which nn is a positive integer. (Some proofs require this restriction.)

By linearity, the formulas of Section 2.1 are implied by the special cases in which ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) and ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) are of the form tkt^{k} for some integer kk, and these special cases (especially k=0k=0 and k=1k=1) are particularly important. These special cases of (2.1.1), (2.1.4), and (2.1.5) are especially useful and may be written

[xn]⁡fk=kn​[tn−k]⁡R​(t)n,where ​n≠0,\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}f^{k}=\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}R(t)^{n},\ \text{where }n\neq 0, (2.2.1)
[xn]⁡fk1−x​R′​(f)=[tn−k]⁡R​(t)n.\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}\frac{f^{k}}{1-xR^{\prime}(f)}=\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}R(t)^{n}. (2.2.2)
[xn]⁡fk1−f​R′​(f)/R⁡(f)=[tn−k]⁡R​(t)n.\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}\frac{f^{k}}{1-fR^{\prime}(f)/R(f)}=\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}{R(t)^{n}}. (2.2.3)

In these formulas, let us assume that R⁡(t)R(t) has constant term 1. (It is not hard to modify our approach to take care of the more general situation in which the constant term of R⁡(t)R(t) is invertible.) Then the coefficient of xx in f⁡(x)f(x) is 1, so f⁡(x)/xf(x)/x has constant term 1. If we set n=m+kn=m+k in (2.2.1), (2.2.2), and (2.2.3) then the results may be written

[xm]⁡(f/x)k=km+k​[tm]⁡R​(t)m+k,where ​m+k≠0,\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{m}]}(f/x)^{k}=\frac{k}{m+k}\mathop{[t^{m}]}R(t)^{m+k},\ \text{where }m+k\neq 0, (2.2.4)
[xm]⁡(f/x)k1−x​R′​(f)=[tm]⁡R​(t)m+k\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{m}]}\frac{(f/x)^{k}}{1-xR^{\prime}(f)}=\mathop{[t^{m}]}R(t)^{m+k} (2.2.5)
[xm]⁡(f/x)k1−f​R′​(f)/R⁡(f)=[tm]⁡R​(t)m+k.\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{m}]}\frac{(f/x)^{k}}{1-fR^{\prime}(f)/R(f)}=\mathop{[t^{m}]}R(t)^{m+k}. (2.2.6)

It is easy to see that in each of these equations, for fixed mm both sides are polynomials in kk. Thus if these equalities hold whenever kk is a positive integer, then they hold as identities of polynomials in kk. Moreover, although (2.2.4) is invalid for k=−mk=-m, if m>0m>0 we may take the limit as k→−mk\to-m with l’Hôpital’s rule to obtain

[xm](f/x)−m=[x0]f−m=−m[tm]logR.\mathop{[x^{m}]}(f/x)^{-m}=\mathop{[x^{0}]}f^{-m}=-m\mathop{[t^{m}]}\log R. (2.2.7)

(Note that (2.2.7) does not hold for m=0m=0.) By linearity, (2.2.7) yields a supplement to (2.1.1) that takes care of the case n=0n=0:

[x0]⁡ϕ⁡(f)=[t0]⁡ϕ⁡(t)+[t−1]⁡ϕ′​(t)​log⁡R.\mathop{[x^{0}]}\phi(f)=\mathop{[t^{0}]}\phi(t)+\mathop{[t^{-1}]}\phi^{\prime}(t)\log R. (2.2.8)

We can also differentiate (2.2.4) with respect to kk and then set k=0k=0 to obtain

[xm]​log⁡(f/x)=1m​[tm]⁡R​(t)m,for m≠0.[x^{m}]\log(f/x)=\frac{1}{m}\mathop{[t^{m}]}R(t)^{m},\ \text{for $m\neq 0$}. (2.2.9)

Returning to (2.2.1)–(2.2.3), we see that if they hold when nn and kk are positive integers, then they also hold when nn and kk are arbitrary integers. (Note that if n<kn<k then everything is zero.)

2.3. A simple example: Catalan numbers

The Catalan numbers CnC_{n} may defined by the equation

c⁡(x)=1+x​c​(x)2c(x)=1+xc(x)^{2} (2.3.1)

for their generating function c⁡(x)=∑n=0∞Cn​xn.c(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}C_{n}x^{n}. The quadratic equation (2.3.1) has two solutions, (1±1−4​x)/(2​x)\bigl(1\pm\sqrt{1-4x}\bigr)/(2x), but only the minus sign gives a power series, so

c⁡(x)=1−1−4​x2​x.c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}.

Unfortunately (2.3.1) is not of the form f⁡(x)=x​R​(f⁡(x))f(x)=xR(f(x)), so we cannot apply directly any of the versions of Lagrange inversion that we have seen so far.

One way to apply Lagrange inversion is to set f⁡(x)=c⁡(x)−1f(x)=c(x)-1, so that f=x​(1+f)2f=x(1+f)^{2}. We may then apply Theorem 2.1.1 to the case R⁡(t)=(1+t)2R(t)=(1+t)^{2}. The equation f=x​(1+f)2f=x(1+f)^{2} has the solution

f⁡(x)=c⁡(x)−1=x​c​(x)2=1−1−4​x2​x−1.f(x)=c(x)-1=xc(x)^{2}=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}-1.

Then (2.1.1) with ϕ⁡(t)=(1+t)k\phi(t)=(1+t)^{k} gives for n>0n>0

[xn]⁡c​(x)k\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}c(x)^{k} =[xn]⁡(1+f)k=1n​[tn−1]⁡k​(1+t)k−1​(1+t)2​n\displaystyle=\mathop{[x^{n}]}(1+f)^{k}=\frac{1}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-1}]}k(1+t)^{k-1}(1+t)^{2n}
=kn​[tn−1]⁡(2​n+k−1n−1).\displaystyle=\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-1}]}\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}.

Thus since the constant term in c​(x)kc(x)^{k} is 1, we have

c​(x)k=1+∑n=1∞kn​(2​n+k−1n−1)​xn.c(x)^{k}=1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}x^{n}.

The sum may also be written

c​(x)k=∑n=0∞k2​n+k​(2​n+kn)​xn=∑n=0∞kn+k​(2​n+k−1n)​xn.c(x)^{k}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{2n+k}\binom{2n+k}{n}x^{n}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n+k}\binom{2n+k-1}{n}x^{n}. (2.3.2)

These formulas are valid for all kk except where n=−k/2n=-k/2 in the first sum in (2.3.2) or n=−kn=-k in the second sum in (2.3.2). These coefficients are called ballot numbers, and for k=1k=1 (2.3.2) gives the usual formula for the Catalan numbers, Cn=1n+1​(2​nn)C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.

Equation (2.1.2) with ϕ⁡(t)=(1+t)k\phi(t)=(1+t)^{k} gives a formula for the ballot number as a difference of two binomial coefficients,

[xn]⁡c​(x)k\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{n}]}c(x)^{k} =[tn]⁡1−t1+t​(1+t)k​(1+t)2​n\displaystyle=\mathop{[t^{n}]}\frac{1-t}{1+t}(1+t)^{k}(1+t)^{2n}
=[tn]⁡(1−t)​(1+t)2​n+k−1\displaystyle=\mathop{[t^{n}]}(1-t)(1+t)^{2n+k-1}
=(2​n+k−1n)−(2​n+k−1n−1),\displaystyle=\binom{2n+k-1}{n}-\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1},

and equation (2.1.3) with ϕ⁡(t)=(1+t)k\phi(t)=(1+t)^{k} gives another such formula,

c​(x)k\displaystyle c(x)^{k} =∑nxn​[tn]⁡((1+t)2​n+k−2​x​(1+t)2​n+k+1)\displaystyle=\sum_{n}x^{n}\mathop{[t^{n}]}\bigl((1+t)^{2n+k}-2x(1+t)^{2n+k+1}\bigr)
=∑nxn​[(2​n+kn)−2​(2​n+k−1n−1)].\displaystyle=\sum_{n}x^{n}\left[\binom{2n+k}{n}-2\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}\right].

Finally, (2.2.9) gives

[xm]⁡log⁡(f/x)=[xm]⁡2​log⁡c⁡(x)=1m​[tm]⁡(1+t)2​m=1m​(2​mm),\mathop{[x^{m}]}\log(f/x)=\mathop{[x^{m}]}2\log c(x)=\frac{1}{m}\mathop{[t^{m}]}(1+t)^{2m}=\frac{1}{m}\binom{2m}{m},

so

log⁡c⁡(x)=∑m=1∞12​m​(2​mm)​xm.\log c(x)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2m}\binom{2m}{m}x^{m}.

Since R⁡(t)=(1+t)2R(t)=(1+t)^{2}, we have R′​(t)=2​(1+t)R^{\prime}(t)=2(1+t), so 1−x​R′​(f)=1−2​x​c​(x)=1−4​x1-xR^{\prime}(f)=1-2xc(x)=\sqrt{1-4x}. Thus (2.1.4), with ψ⁡(t)=(1+t)k\psi(t)=(1+t)^{k} gives

[xn]⁡c​(x)k1−4​x=[tn]⁡(1+t)k​(1+t)2​n=(2​n+kk),\mathop{[x^{n}]}\frac{c(x)^{k}}{\sqrt{1-4x}}=\mathop{[t^{n}]}(1+t)^{k}(1+t)^{2n}=\binom{2n+k}{k},

so

c​(x)k1−4​x=∑n=0∞(2​n+kk)​xn.\frac{c(x)^{k}}{\sqrt{1-4x}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{2n+k}{k}x^{n}. (2.3.3)

Equating coefficients of xnx^{n} in c​(x)k​c​(x)l=c​(x)k+lc(x)^{k}c(x)^{l}=c(x)^{k+l}, and using (2.3.2), gives the convolution identity

∑i+j=nk2​i+k​(2​i+ki)⋅l2​j+l​(2​j+lj)=k+l2​n+k+l​(2​n+k+ln).\sum_{i+j=n}\frac{k}{2i+k}\binom{2i+k}{i}\cdot\frac{l}{2j+l}\binom{2j+l}{j}=\frac{k+l}{2n+k+l}\binom{2n+k+l}{n}.

Similarly using (2.3.2) and (2.3.3) we get

∑i+j=nk2​i+k​(2​i+ki)​(2​j+lj)=(2​n+k+ln).\sum_{i+j=n}\frac{k}{2i+k}\binom{2i+k}{i}\binom{2j+l}{j}=\binom{2n+k+l}{n}.

These convolution identities are special cases of identities discussed in section 3.3.

Exercise 2.3.1.

Derive these formulas for c⁡(x)c(x) in other ways by applying Lagrange inversion to the equations f=x/(1−f)f=x/(1-f) and f=x⁡(1+f2)f=x(1+f^{2}).

2.4. A generalization

There is another way to apply Lagrange inversion to the equation c⁡(x)=1+x​c​(x)2c(x)=1+xc(x)^{2} that, while very simple, has far-reaching consequences. Consider the equation

F=z⁡(1+x​F2)F=z(1+xF^{2}) (2.4.1)

where we think of FF as a power series in zz with coefficients that are polynomials in xx. We may apply (2.2.1) to (2.4.1) to get

[zn]⁡Fk=kn​[tn−k]⁡(1+x​t2)n.\mathop{[z^{n}]}F^{k}=\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}(1+xt^{2})^{n}.

The right side is 0 unless n−kn-k is even, and for n=2​m+kn=2m+k we have

[z2​m+k]⁡Fk=k2​m+k​[t2​m]⁡(1+x​t2)2​m+k=k2​m+k​(2​m+km)​xm.\mathop{[z^{2m+k}]}F^{k}=\frac{k}{2m+k}\mathop{[t^{2m}]}(1+xt^{2})^{2m+k}=\frac{k}{2m+k}\binom{2m+k}{m}x^{m}.

Thus we have (if kk is an integer but not a negative even integer)

Fk=∑m=0∞k2​m+k​(2​m+km)​xm​z2​m+k.F^{k}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{2m+k}\binom{2m+k}{m}x^{m}z^{2m+k}. (2.4.2)

Now let cc be the result of setting z=1z=1 in FF (an admissible substitution), so by (2.4.2), we have

ck=∑m=0∞k2​m+k​(2​m+km)​xmc^{k}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{2m+k}\binom{2m+k}{m}x^{m}

and by (2.4.1) we have c=1+x​c2c=1+xc^{2}. Moreover, as we have seen before, c=1+x​c2c=1+xc^{2} has a unique power series solution.

The same idea works much more generally, but we must take care that the substitution is admissible. For example, we can solve f=x⁡(1+f)f=x(1+f) by Lagrange inversion, but we cannot set x=1x=1 in the solution.

The case in which the coefficients of R⁡(t)R(t) are indeterminates is easy to deal with.

Theorem 2.4.1.

Suppose that R⁡(t)=∑n=0∞rn​tnR(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r_{n}t^{n}, where the rnr_{n} are indeterminates. Then there is a unique power series ff satisfying f=R⁡(f)f=R(f). If ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) is a power series then

ϕ⁡(f)=ϕ⁡(0)+∑n=1∞1n​[tn−1]⁡ϕ′​(t)​R​(t)n,\phi(f)=\phi(0)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-1}]}\phi^{\prime}(t)R(t)^{n}, (2.4.3)

and for any Laurent series ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) and ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) we have

ϕ⁡(f)=[t0]⁡ϕ⁡(t)+[t−1]⁡ϕ′​(t)​log⁡(R/r0)+∑n≠01n​[tn−1]⁡ϕ′​(t)​R​(t)n,\displaystyle\phi(f)=\mathop{[t^{0}]}\phi(t)+\mathop{[t^{-1}]}\phi^{\prime}(t)\log(R/r_{0})+\sum_{n\neq 0}\frac{1}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-1}]}\phi^{\prime}(t)R(t)^{n}, (2.4.4)
ϕ⁡(f)=∑n[tn]⁡(1−t​R′​(t)/R⁡(t))​ϕ​(t)​R​(t)n=∑n[tn]⁡(1−R′​(t))​ϕ​(t)​R​(t)n,\displaystyle\phi(f)=\sum_{n}\mathop{[t^{n}]}\bigl(1-tR^{\prime}(t)/R(t)\bigr)\phi(t)R(t)^{n}=\sum_{n}\mathop{[t^{n}]}(1-R^{\prime}(t))\phi(t)R(t)^{n}, (2.4.5)
ψ⁡(f)1−R′​(f)=ψ⁡(f)1−f​R′​(f)/R⁡(f)=∑n[tn]⁡ψ⁡(t)​R​(t)n.\displaystyle\frac{\psi(f)}{1-R^{\prime}(f)}=\frac{\psi(f)}{1-fR^{\prime}(f)/R(f)}=\sum_{n}\mathop{[t^{n}]}{\psi(t)R(t)^{n}}. (2.4.6)

In (2.4.5) and (2.4.6) the sum is over all integers nn.

Proof.

These formulas follow from equations (2.1.1) to (2.1.5) on making the admissible substitution x=1x=1, where for (2.4.4) we have included the correction term given by (2.2.8), modified to take into account that the constant term of R⁡(t)R(t) is r0r_{0} rather than 1. Uniqueness follows by equating coefficients of the monomials r0i0r1i1⋯r_{0}^{i_{0}}r_{1}^{i_{1}}\cdots on both sides of f=R⁡(f)f=R(f), which gives a recurrence that determines them uniquely.∎

We would like to relax the requirement in Theorem 2.4.1 that the rnr_{n} be indeterminates. To do this, we can take any of the formulas of Theorem 2.4.1 and apply any admissible substitution for the rnr_{n}. For example, the following result, while not the most general possible, is sometimes useful.

Theorem 2.4.2.

Suppose that R⁡(t)=∑n=0∞rn​tnR(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r_{n}t^{n}, where the coefficients lie in some power series ring C⁡[[u1,u2,…]]C[[u_{1},u_{2},\dots]], and that each rnr_{n} with n>0n>0 is divisible by some uiu_{i}. Then there is a unique power series ff satisfying f=R⁡(f)f=R(f), and formulas (2.4.3) to (2.4.6) hold.∎

We note that more generally, any admissible substitution will yield a solution of f=R⁡(f)f=R(f) to which these formulas hold, but uniqueness is not guaranteed. For example, the equation f=x+y​f2f=x+yf^{2} has the unique power series solution,

f=1−1−4​x​y2​y=∑n=0∞1n+1​(2​nn)​xn+1​yn.f=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4xy}}{2y}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}x^{n+1}y^{n}.

The admissible substitution y=1y=1 gives f=12​(1−1−4​x)f=\frac{1}{2}(1-\sqrt{1-4x}) as a power series solution of the equation f=x+f2f=x+f^{2}. However, the equation f=x+f2f=x+f^{2} has another power series solution, f=12​(1+1−4​x).f=\frac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{1-4x}).

Exercise 2.4.3.

The equation f=x+f2f=x+f^{2} has two power series solutions, f=12​(1±1−4​x)f=\frac{1}{2}(1\pm\sqrt{1-4x}). However, according to Theorem 2.1.1, the equivalent equation f=x/(1−f)f=x/(1-f) has only one power series solution. Explain the discrepancy.

2.5. Explicit formulas for the coefficients

It is sometimes useful to have an explicit formula for the coefficients of fkf^{k} where f=x​R​(f)f=xR(f). With R⁡(t)=∑n=0∞rn​tnR(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r_{n}t^{n}, if we expand R​(t)nR(t)^{n} by the multinomial theorem then (2.2.1) gives

fk=∑n0+n1+⋯=nn1+2​n2+3​n3+⋯=n−kk(n−1)!n0!​n1!​…r0n0r1n1⋯xn.f^{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{0}+n_{1}+\cdots=n\\ n_{1}+2n_{2}+3n_{3}+\cdots=n-k\end{subarray}}k\frac{(n-1)!}{n_{0}!\,n_{1}!\dots}r_{0}^{n_{0}}r_{1}^{n_{1}}\cdots x^{n}. (2.5.1)

We might also want to express the coefficients of fkf^{k} in terms of the coefficients of g=f⟨−1⟩g=f^{\langle-1\rangle}. Suppose that g⁡(x)=x−g2​x2−g3​x3−⋯g(x)=x-g_{2}x^{2}-g_{3}x^{3}-\cdots, where the minus signs and the assumption that the coefficient of xx in gg is 1 make our formula simpler with no real loss of generality. Then (2.2.1) gives

[xm]​fk=km​[tm−k]​(11−g2​t−g3​t2−⋯)m.[x^{m}]f^{k}=\frac{k}{m}[t^{m-k}]\left(\frac{1}{1-g_{2}t-g_{3}t^{2}-\cdots}\right)^{m}.

Expanding by the binomial theorem and simplifying gives

fk=∑n2+n3+⋯=n−mn2+2​n3+⋯=m−kk(n−1)!m!n2!n3!⋯g2n2g3n3⋯xmf^{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{2}+n_{3}+\cdots=n-m\\ n_{2}+2n_{3}+\cdots=m-k\end{subarray}}k\frac{(n-1)!}{m!\,n_{2}!\,n_{3}!\cdots}g_{2}^{n_{2}}g_{3}^{n_{3}}\cdots x^{m}

where the sum is over all mm, nn, and n2,n3,…n_{2},n_{3},\dots satisfying the two subscripted equalities. If we replace mm with n0n_{0} then we may write the formula as

fk=∑n0+n2+n3+⋯=n2​n2+3​n3+⋯=n−kk(n−1)!n0!n2!n3!⋯xn0g2n2g3n3⋯f^{k}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{0}+n_{2}+n_{3}+\cdots=n\\ 2n_{2}+3n_{3}+\cdots=n-k\end{subarray}}k\frac{(n-1)!}{n_{0}!\,n_{2}!\,n_{3}!\cdots}x^{n_{0}}g_{2}^{n_{2}}g_{3}^{n_{3}}\cdots (2.5.2)

and we see that the coefficients here are exactly the same as the coefficients in (2.5.1) (with n1=0n_{1}=0).

Exercise 2.5.1.

Explain the connection between (2.5.1) and (2.5.2) without using Lagrange inversion.

2.6. Derivative formulas

Lagrange inversion, especially in its analytic formulations, is often stated in terms of derivatives. We give here several derivative forms of Lagrange inversion.

Theorem 2.6.1.

Let G⁡(t)=∑n=0∞gn​tnG(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}g_{n}t^{n}, where the gig_{i} are indeterminates. Then there is a unique power series ff satisfying

f=x+G⁡(f)f=x+G(f)

and for any power series ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) and ψ⁡(t)\psi(t) we have

ϕ⁡(f)=∑m=0∞dmd​xm​(ϕ⁡(x)​(1−G′​(x))​G​(x)mm!),\phi(f)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{d^{m}\ }{dx^{m}}\left(\phi(x)\bigl(1-G^{\prime}(x)\bigr)\frac{G(x)^{m}}{m!}\right), (2.6.1)
ϕ⁡(f)=ϕ⁡(x)+∑m=1∞dm−1d​xm−1​(ϕ′​(x)​G​(x)mm!),\phi(f)=\phi(x)+\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{d^{m-1}\ }{dx^{m-1}}\left(\phi^{\prime}(x)\frac{G(x)^{m}}{m!}\right), (2.6.2)

and

ψ⁡(f)1−G′​(f)=∑m=0∞dmd​xm​(ψ⁡(x)​G​(x)mm!).\frac{\psi(f)}{1-G^{\prime}(f)}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{d^{m}\ }{dx^{m}}\left(\psi(x)\frac{G(x)^{m}}{m!}\right). (2.6.3)
Proof.

We first prove (2.6.3). By (2.4.6) we have

ψ⁡(f)1−G′​(f)=∑n=0∞[tn]⁡ψ⁡(t)​(x+G⁡(t))n=∑m=0∞∑n=0∞[tn]⁡(nm)​xn−m​ψ​(t)​G​(t)m.\frac{\psi(f)}{1-G^{\prime}(f)}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathop{[t^{n}]}\psi(t)(x+G(t))^{n}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathop{[t^{n}]}\binom{n}{m}x^{n-m}\psi(t)G(t)^{m}.

So to prove (2.6.3), it suffices to prove that

dmd​xm​(ψ⁡(x)​G​(x)mm!)=∑n=0∞[tn]⁡(nm)​xn−m​ψ​(t)​G​(t)m.\frac{d^{m}\ }{dx^{m}}\left(\psi(x)\frac{G(x)^{m}}{m!}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathop{[t^{n}]}\binom{n}{m}x^{n-m}\psi(t)G(t)^{m}.

We show more generally, that for any power series α⁡(t)\alpha(t) we have

dmd​xm​α⁡(x)m!=∑n=0∞[tn]⁡(nm)​xn−m​α​(t).\frac{d^{m}\ }{dx^{m}}\frac{\alpha(x)}{m!}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathop{[t^{n}]}\binom{n}{m}x^{n-m}\alpha(t). (2.6.4)

But by linearity, it is sufficient to prove (2.6.4) for the case α⁡(t)=tj\alpha(t)=t^{j}, where both sides are equal to (jm)​xj−m\binom{j}{m}x^{j-m}.

Next, (2.6.1) follows from (2.6.3) by taking ψ⁡(t)=(1−G′​(t))​ϕ​(t)\psi(t)=(1-G^{\prime}(t))\phi(t).

Finally, we derive (2.6.2) from (2.6.1). Writing DD for d/d​xd/dx, ϕ\phi for ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) and GG for G⁡(x)G(x), we have

Dm​(ϕ​Gmm!)=Dm−1​(D⁡(ϕ​Gm)m!)=Dm−1​(ϕ′​Gmm!+ϕ​G′​Gm−1(m−1)!).D^{m}\left(\phi\frac{G^{m}}{m!}\right)=D^{m-1}\left(\frac{D(\phi G^{m})}{m!}\right)=D^{m-1}\left(\phi^{\prime}\frac{G^{m}}{m!}+\phi G^{\prime}\frac{G^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\right).

Thus

Dm−1​(ϕ′​Gmm!)=Dm​(ϕ​Gmm!)−Dm−1​(ϕ​G′​Gm−1(m−1)!),D^{m-1}\left(\phi^{\prime}\frac{G^{m}}{m!}\right)=D^{m}\left(\phi\frac{G^{m}}{m!}\right)-D^{m-1}\left(\phi G^{\prime}\frac{G^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\right),

so

ϕ+∑m=1∞Dm−1​(ϕ′​Gmm!)=∑m=0∞Dm​(ϕ​Gmm!)−∑m=0∞Dm​(ϕ​G′​Gmm!).∎\phi+\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}D^{m-1}\left(\phi^{\prime}\frac{G^{m}}{m!}\right)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}D^{m}\left(\phi\frac{G^{m}}{m!}\right)-\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}D^{m}\left(\phi G^{\prime}\frac{G^{m}}{m!}\right).\qed

As before, applying an admissible substitution allows more general coefficients to be used.

As an application of these formulas, let us take G⁡(x)=z​H​(x)G(x)=zH(x) and consider the formula

ϕ⁡(f)⋅ψ⁡(f)1−z​H′​(f)=ϕ⁡(f)​ψ​(f)1−z​H′​(f).\phi(f)\cdot\frac{\psi(f)}{1-zH^{\prime}(f)}=\frac{\phi(f)\psi(f)}{1-zH^{\prime}(f)}.

Applying (2.6.2) and (2.6.3) to the left side and (2.6.3) to the right, and then equating coefficients of znz^{n} gives the convolution identity

∑m=0n(nm)​dm−1d​xm−1​(ϕ′​(x)​H​(x)m)​dn−md​xn−m​(ψ⁡(x)​H​(x)n−m)=dnd​xn​(ϕ⁡(x)​ψ​(x)​H​(x)n)\sum_{m=0}^{n}\binom{n}{m}\frac{d^{m-1}\ }{dx^{m-1}}\left(\phi^{\prime}(x)H(x)^{m}\right)\frac{d^{n-m}\ }{dx^{n-m}}\left(\psi(x)H(x)^{n-m}\right)=\frac{d^{n}\ }{dx^{n}}\bigl(\phi(x)\psi(x)H(x)^{n}\bigr) (2.6.5)

and similarly, expanding ϕ⁡(f)​ψ​(f)\phi(f)\psi(f) in two ways using (2.6.2) gives

∑m=0n(nm)​dm−1d​xm−1​(ϕ′​(x)​H​(x)m)​dn−m−1d​xn−m−1​(ψ′​(x)​H​(x)n−m)=dn−1d​xn−1​((ϕ⁡(x)​ψ​(x))′​H​(x)n).\sum_{m=0}^{n}\binom{n}{m}\frac{d^{m-1}\ }{dx^{m-1}}\left(\phi^{\prime}(x)H(x)^{m}\right)\frac{d^{n-m-1}\ }{dx^{n-m-1}}\left(\psi^{\prime}(x)H(x)^{n-m}\right)=\frac{d^{n-1}\ }{dx^{n-1}}\bigl((\phi(x)\psi(x))^{\prime}H(x)^{n}\bigr). (2.6.6)

Here dm−1​ϕ′​(x)/d​xm−1d^{m-1}\phi^{\prime}(x)/dx^{m-1} for m=0m=0 is to be interpreted as ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). Formulas (2.6.5) and (2.6.6) were found by Cauchy [10]; a formula equivalent to (2.6.5) had been found earlier by Pfaff [58]. A detailed historical discussion of these identities and generalizations has been given by Johnson [40]; see also Chu [12, 14] and Abel [2]. Our approach to these identities has also been given by Huang and Ma [36].

Exercise 2.6.2.

With the notation of Theorem 2.6.1, show that for any positive integer kk,

G​(f)k=∑m=0∞k(m+k)​m!​dmd​xm​G​(x)m+k.G(f)^{k}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{(m+k)\,m!}\frac{d^{m}\ }{dx^{m}}G(x)^{m+k}.

3. Applications

In this section we describe some applications of Lagrange inversion.

3.1. A rational function expansion

It is surprising that Lagrange inversion can give interesting results when the solution to the equation to be solved is rational.

We consider the equation

f=1+a+a​b​f,f=1+a+abf,

with solution

f=1+a1−a​b.f=\frac{1+a}{1-ab}.

We apply (2.4.6) with R⁡(t)=1+a+a​b​tR(t)=1+a+abt and ψ⁡(t)=tr​(1+b​t)s\psi(t)=t^{r}(1+bt)^{s}. Here we have 1+b​f=(1+b)/(1−a​b)1+bf=(1+b)/(1-ab) and 1−R′​(f)=1−a​b1-R^{\prime}(f)=1-ab. Then

(1+a)r​(1+b)s(1−a​b)r+s+1\displaystyle\frac{(1+a)^{r}(1+b)^{s}}{(1-ab)^{r+s+1}} =∑n[tn]​tr​(1+b​t)s​(1+a+a​b​t)n\displaystyle=\sum_{n}[t^{n}]t^{r}(1+bt)^{s}(1+a+abt)^{n}
=∑n,i[tn]​(ni)​ai​tr​(1+b​t)s+i\displaystyle=\sum_{n,i}[t^{n}]\binom{n}{i}a^{i}t^{r}(1+bt)^{s+i}
=∑n,i,j[tn]​(ni)​ai​(s+ij)​bj​tr+j\displaystyle=\sum_{n,i,j}[t^{n}]\binom{n}{i}a^{i}\binom{s+i}{j}b^{j}t^{r+j}
=∑i,j(r+ji)​(s+ij)​ai​bj.\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\binom{r+j}{i}\binom{s+i}{j}a^{i}b^{j}.

For another approach to this identity, see Gessel and Stanton [26].

3.2. The tree function

In applying Lagrange inversion, the nicest examples are those in which the series R⁡(t)R(t) has the property that there is a simple formula for the coefficients of R​(t)nR(t)^{n}, and these simple formulas usually come from the exponential function or the binomial theorem. In this section we discuss the simplest case, in which R⁡(t)=etR(t)=e^{t}. Later, in section 3.5, we discuss a more complicated example involving the exponential function.

Let T⁡(x)T(x) be the power series satisfying

T⁡(x)=x​eT⁡(x).T(x)=xe^{T(x)}.

Equivalently, T⁡(x)=(x​e−x)⟨−1⟩T(x)=(xe^{-x})^{\langle-1\rangle} and thus T⁡(x​e−x)=xT(xe^{-x})=x. Then by the properties of exponential generating functions (see, e.g., Stanley [70, Chapter 5]), T⁡(x)T(x) is the exponential generating function for rooted trees and eT⁡(x)=T⁡(x)/xe^{T(x)}=T(x)/x is the exponential generating function for forests of rooted trees. We shall call T⁡(x)T(x) the tree function and we shall call F⁡(x)=eT⁡(x)F(x)=e^{T(x)} the forest function The tree function is closely related to the Lambert WW function [16, 17] which may be defined by W⁡(x)=−T⁡(−x)W(x)=-T(-x). Although the Lambert WW function is better known, we will state our results in terms of the tree and forest functions.

Applying (2.2.1) with R⁡(t)=etR(t)=e^{t} gives

T⁡(x)=∑n=1∞nn−1​xnn!T(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{n-1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!} (3.2.1)

and more generally,

T​(x)kk!=∑n=k∞k​nn−k−1​(nk)​xnn!\frac{T(x)^{k}}{k!}=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}kn^{n-k-1}\binom{n}{k}\frac{x^{n}}{n!} (3.2.2)

for all positive integers kk, and

F​(x)k=ek​T​(x)=∑n=0∞k​(n+k)n−1​xnn!F(x)^{k}=e^{kT(x)}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}k(n+k)^{n-1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!} (3.2.3)

for all kk. Equation (3.2.2) implies that there are k​nn−k−1​(nk)kn^{n-k-1}\binom{n}{k} forests of nn rooted trees on nn vertices and equation (3.2.3) implies that there are k​(n+k)n−1k(n+k)^{n-1} forests with vertex set {1,2,…,n+k}\{1,2,\dots,n+k\} in which the roots are 1, 2, …, kk.

An interesting special case of (3.2.3) is k=−1k=-1, which may be rearranged to

F⁡(x)=(1−∑n=1∞(n−1)n−1​xnn!)−1.F(x)=\biggl(1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(n-1)^{n-1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}\biggr)^{-1}. (3.2.4)

Equation (3.2.4) may be interpreted in terms of prime parking functions [70, Exercise 5.49f, p. 95; Solution, p. 141].

Applying (2.2.6) gives

F​(x)k1−T⁡(x)=∑n=0∞(n+k)n​xnn!.\frac{F(x)^{k}}{1-T(x)}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}. (3.2.5)

A. Lacasse [46, p. 90] conjectured an identity that may be written as

U​(x)3−U​(x)2=∑n=0∞nn+1​xnn!,U(x)^{3}-U(x)^{2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n^{n+1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}, (3.2.6)

where

U⁡(x)=∑n=0∞nn​xnn!.U(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n^{n}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}.

Proofs of Lacasse’s conjecture were given by Chen et al. [11], Prodinger [59], Sun [73], and Younsi [80]. We will prove (3.2.6) by showing that both sides are equal to T⁡(x)/(1−T⁡(x))3T(x)/(1-T(x))^{3}.

To do this, we first note that the right side of (3.2.6) is

dd​x​∑n=0∞(n−1)n​xnn!=dd​x​e−T⁡(x)1−T⁡(x)=e−T⁡(x)​T​(x)​T′​(x)(1−T⁡(x))2.\frac{d\ }{dx}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n-1)^{n}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}=\frac{d\ }{dx}\frac{e^{-T(x)}}{1-T(x)}=\frac{e^{-T(x)}T(x)T^{\prime}(x)}{(1-T(x))^{2}}. (3.2.7)

Differentiating (3.2.1) with respect to xx gives

T′​(x)=∑n=0∞(n+1)n​xnn!,T^{\prime}(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+1)^{n}\frac{x^{n}}{n!},

which by (3.2.5) is equal to eT⁡(x)/(1−T⁡(x))e^{T(x)}/(1-T(x)). Thus (3.2.7) is equal to T⁡(x)/(1−T⁡(x))3T(x)/(1-T(x))^{3}. But by (3.2.5), U⁡(x)=1/(1−T⁡(x))U(x)=1/(1-T(x)) from which it follows easily that U​(x)3−U​(x)2=T⁡(x)/(1−T⁡(x))3U(x)^{3}-U(x)^{2}=T(x)/(1-T(x))^{3}.

The series T⁡(x)T(x) and U⁡(x)U(x) were studied by Zvonkine [79], who showed that Dk​U​(x)D^{k}U(x) and Dk​U​(x)2D^{k}U(x)^{2}, where D=x​d/d​xD=xd/dx, are polynomials in U⁡(x)U(x).

The series ∑n=0∞(n+k)n+m​xn/n!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n+m}x^{n}\!/n!, where mm is an arbitrary integer, can be expressed in terms of T⁡(x)T(x). (The case k=0k=0 has been studied by Smiley [67].) We first deal with the case in which mm is negative.

Theorem 3.2.1.

Let ll be a positive integer. Then for some polynomial pl​(u)p_{l}(u) of degree l−1l-1, with coefficients that are rational functions of kk, we have

∑n=0∞(n+k)n−l​xnn!=ek​T​(x)​pl​(T⁡(x)).\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n-l}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}=e^{kT(x)}p_{l}(T(x)). (3.2.8)

The first three polynomials pl​(u)p_{l}(u) are

p1​(u)\displaystyle p_{1}(u) =1k,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k},
p2​(u)\displaystyle p_{2}(u) =1k2−uk⁡(k+1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k^{2}}-\frac{u}{k(k+1)},
p3​(u)\displaystyle p_{3}(u) =1k3−(2​k+1)k2​(k+1)2​u+u2k​(k+1)​(k+2).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k^{3}}-\frac{(2k+1)}{k^{2}(k+1)^{2}}u+\frac{u^{2}}{k(k+1)(k+2)}.

Before proving Theorem 3.2.1 let us check (3.2.8) for l=1l=1 and l=2l=2. The case l=1l=1 is equivalent to (3.2.3). For l=2l=2, we have

ek​T​(x)=F​(x)k=k​∑n=0∞(n+k)n−1​xnn!e^{kT(x)}=F(x)^{k}=k\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n-1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}

and

ek​T​(x)​T​(x)\displaystyle e^{kT(x)}T(x) =F​(x)k⋅x​F​(x)=x​F​(x)k+1\displaystyle=F(x)^{k}\cdot xF(x)=xF(x)^{k+1}
=x⁡(k+1)​∑n=0∞(n+k+1)n−1​xnn!\displaystyle=x(k+1)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k+1)^{n-1}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}
=(k+1)​∑n=0∞n​(n+k)n−2​xnn!.\displaystyle=(k+1)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n(n+k)^{n-2}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}.

Thus

ek​T​(x)​(1k2−T⁡(x)k⁡(k+1))\displaystyle e^{kT(x)}\left(\frac{1}{k^{2}}-\frac{T(x)}{k(k+1)}\right) =1k​∑n=0∞((n+k)n−1−n​(n+k)n−2)​xnn!\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\bigl((n+k)^{n-1}-n(n+k)^{n-2}\bigr)\frac{x^{n}}{n!}
=∑n=0∞(n+k)n−2​xnn!.\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n-2}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}.

The general case can be proved in a similar way. (See Exercise 3.2.4.) However, it is instructive to take a different approach, using finite differences (cf. Gould [31]), that we we will use again in section 3.3.

Let ss be a function defined on the nonnegative integers. The shift operator EE takes ss to the function E​sEs defined by (E​s)​(n)=s​(n+1)(Es)(n)=s(n+1). We denote by II the identity operator that takes ss to itself and by Δ\Delta the difference operator E−IE-I, so (Δ​s)​(n)=s⁡(n+1)−s⁡(n)(\Delta s)(n)=s(n+1)-s(n). It is easily verified that if ss is a polynomial of degree d>0d>0 with leading coefficient LL then Δ​s\Delta s is a polynomial of degree d−1d-1 with leading coefficient d​LdL, and if ss is a constant then Δ​s=0\Delta s=0. The kkth difference of ss is the function Δk​s\Delta^{k}s. Thus if ss is a polynomial of degree dd with leading coefficient LL then Δk​s=0\Delta^{k}s=0 for k>dk>d and Δd​s\Delta^{d}s is the constant d!​Ld!\,L.

Since the operators EE and II commute, we can expand Δk=(E−I)k\Delta^{k}=(E-I)^{k} by the binomial theorem to obtain

(Δk​s)​(n)=∑i=0k(−1)k−i​(ki)​s​(n+i).(\Delta^{k}s)(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{k-i}\binom{k}{i}s(n+i).

We may summarize the result of this discussion in the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2.2.

Let ss be a polynomial of degree dd with leading coefficient LL. Then

∑i=0k(−1)k−i​(ki)​s​(n+i)\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{k-i}\binom{k}{i}s(n+i)

is 0 if k>dk>d and is the constant d!​Ld!\,L for k=dk=d. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.2.1.

If we set x=u​e−ux=ue^{-u} in Theorem 3.2.1 and use the fact that T⁡(u​e−u)=uT(ue^{-u})=u we see that Theorem (3.2.1) is equivalent to the formula

e−k​u​∑n=0∞(n+k)n−l​(u​e−u)nn!=pl​(u).e^{-ku}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n-l}\frac{(ue^{-u})^{n}}{n!}=p_{l}(u).

We have

e−k​u​∑n=0∞(n+k)n+m​(u​e−u)nn!\displaystyle e^{-ku}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n+m}\frac{(ue^{-u})^{n}}{n!} =∑n=0∞(n+k)n+m​unn!​e−(n+k)​u\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n+m}\frac{u^{n}}{n!}e^{-(n+k)u} (3.2.9)
=∑j=0∞ujj!​∑n=0j(−1)j−n​(jn)​(n+k)j+m\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{u^{j}}{j!}\sum_{n=0}^{j}(-1)^{j-n}\binom{j}{n}(n+k)^{j+m}

If m=−lm=-l is a negative integer and j≥lj\geq l then (n+k)j+m=(n+k)j−l(n+k)^{j+m}=(n+k)^{j-l} is a polynomial in nn of degree less than jj, so the inner sum in (3.2.9) is 0. Thus (3.2.8) follows, with

pl​(u)=∑j=0l−1ujj!​∑n=0j(−1)j−n​(jn)​(n+k)−(l−j).∎p_{l}(u)=\sum_{j=0}^{l-1}\frac{u^{j}}{j!}\sum_{n=0}^{j}(-1)^{j-n}\binom{j}{n}(n+k)^{-(l-j)}.\qed

We cannot set k=0k=0 in (3.2.8), since the n=0n=0 term on the left is k−lk^{-l}. However it is not hard to evaluate ∑n=1∞nn−l​xn/n!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{n-l}x^{n}\!/n!.

Theorem 3.2.3.

Let ql​(u)q_{l}(u) be the result of setting k=1k=1 in pl​(u)p_{l}(u). Then

∑n=1∞nn−l​xnn!=T⁡(x)​ql​(T⁡(x)).\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{n-l}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}=T(x)q_{l}(T(x)).
Proof.

We have

∑n=1∞nn−l​xnn!=x​∑n=0∞(n+1)n−l​xnn!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{n-l}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}=x\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+1)^{n-l}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}

By (3.2.8) with k=1k=1 this is

x​eT⁡(x)​ql​(T⁡(x))=T⁡(x)​ql​(T⁡(x)).xe^{T(x)}q_{l}(T(x))=T(x)q_{l}(T(x)).

∎

Exercise 3.2.4.

Prove Theorem 3.2.1 by finding a formula for the coefficient tj​(n)t_{j}(n) of xn/n!x^{n}\!/n! in ek​T​(x)​T​(x)je^{kT(x)}T(x)^{j} and showing that (n+k)n−l(n+k)^{n-l} can be expressed as a linear combination, with coefficients that are rational functions of kk, of t0​(n),…,tl−1​(n)t_{0}(n),\dots,t_{l-1}(n).

Next we consider ∑n=0∞(n+k)n+m​xn/n!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n+m}x^{n}\!/n! where mm is a nonnegative integer. (We evaluated the case k=0,m=1k=0,m=1 in our discussion of Lacasse’s conjecture.)

Theorem 3.2.5.

Let mm be a nonnegative integer. Then there exists a polynomial rm​(u,k)r_{m}(u,k), with integer coefficients, of degree mm in uu and degree mm in kk, such that

∑n=0∞(n+k)n+m​xnn!=ek​T​(x)​rm​(T​(x),k)(1−T⁡(x))2​m+1.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n+m}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}=e^{kT(x)}\frac{r_{m}(T(x),k)}{(1-T(x))^{2m+1}}.

The first three polynomials rm​(u,k)r_{m}(u,k) are

r0​(u,k)\displaystyle r_{0}(u,k) =1,\displaystyle=1,
r1​(u,k)\displaystyle r_{1}(u,k) =k+(1−k)​u,\displaystyle=k+(1-k)u,
r2​(u,k)\displaystyle r_{2}(u,k) =k2+(1+3​k−2​k2)​u+(2−3​k+k2)​u2.\displaystyle=k^{2}+(1+3k-2k^{2})u+(2-3k+k^{2})u^{2}.
Proof sketch.

We give here a sketch of a proof that tells us something interesting about the polynomials rm​(u,k)r_{m}(u,k); for a more direct approach see Exercise 3.2.6.

As in the proof of Theorem 3.2.1 we set x=u​e−ux=ue^{-u} and consider the sum on the left side of (3.2.9).

Following Carlitz [9], we define the weighted Stirling numbers of the second kind R⁡(n,j,k)R(n,j,k) by

R⁡(n,j,k)=1j!​∑i=0j(−1)j−i​(ji)​(k+i)n,R(n,j,k)=\frac{1}{j!}\sum_{i=0}^{j}(-1)^{j-i}\binom{j}{i}(k+i)^{n},

so that

∑n=0∞R⁡(n,j,k)​xnn!=ek​x​(ex−1)jj!.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R(n,j,k)\frac{x^{n}}{n!}=e^{kx}\frac{(e^{x}-1)^{j}}{j!}. (3.2.10)

(For k=0k=0, R⁡(n,j,k)R(n,j,k) reduces to the ordinary Stirling number of the second kind S⁡(n,j)S(n,j).) Equation (3.2.10) implies that the R⁡(n,j,k)R(n,j,k) is a polynomial in kk with integer coefficients. Then (3.2.9) is equal to ∑j=0∞R⁡(j+m,j,k)​uj.\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}R(j+m,j,k)u^{j}. It is not hard to show that for fixed mm, R⁡(j+m,j,k)R(j+m,j,k) is a polynomial in jj of degree 2​m2m.

Thus

∑j=0∞R⁡(j+m,j,k)​uj=rm​(u,k)(1−u)2​m+1\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}R(j+m,j,k)u^{j}=\frac{r_{m}(u,k)}{(1-u)^{2m+1}}

for some polynomial rm​(u,k)r_{m}(u,k) of degree at most 2​m2m.

We omit the proof that rm​(u,k)r_{m}(u,k) actually has degree mm in uu. ∎

For k=1k=1, the coefficients of rm​(u,1)r_{m}(u,1) are positive integers, sometimes called second-order Eulerian numbers; see, for example, [32, p. 270] and [24].

Exercise 3.2.6.

Give an inductive proof of Theorem 3.2.5 using the fact that if W⁡(m,k)=∑n=0∞(n+k)n+m​xn/n!W(m,k)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+k)^{n+m}x^{n}\!/n! then d​W​(m,k)/d​x=W⁡(m+1,k+1)dW(m,k)/dx=W(m+1,k+1).

We can get convolution identities by applying (3.2.3) and (3.2.5) to

F​(x)k+l1−T⁡(x)=F​(x)k​F​(x)l1−T⁡(x)\frac{F(x)^{k+l}}{1-T(x)}=F(x)^{k}\frac{F(x)^{l}}{1-T(x)}

and

F​(x)k+l=F​(x)k​F​(x)l.F(x)^{k+l}=F(x)^{k}F(x)^{l}.

The first identity yields

(n+k+l)n=∑i=0n(ni)​k​(i+k)i−1​(n−i+l)n−i.(n+k+l)^{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}k(i+k)^{i-1}(n-i+l)^{n-i}.

and the second yields

(k+l)​(n+k+l)n−1=∑i=0n(ni)​k​(i+k)i−1​l​(n−i+l)n−i−1.(k+l)(n+k+l)^{n-1}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}k(i+k)^{i-1}l(n-i+l)^{n-i-1}.

Note that these are identities of polynomials in kk and ll. If we set k=xk=x and l=y−nl=y-n in the first formula we get the nicer looking

(x+y)n=∑i=0n(ni)​x​(x+i)i−1​(y−i)n−i.(x+y)^{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}x(x+i)^{i-1}(y-i)^{n-i}. (3.2.11)

Replacing xx with x/zx/z and yy with y/zy/z in (3.2.11), and multiplying through by znz^{n} gives the homogeneous form

(x+y)n=∑i=0n(ni)​x​(x+i​z)i−1​(y−i​z)n−i(x+y)^{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}x(x+iz)^{i-1}(y-iz)^{n-i} (3.2.12)

which was proved by N. H. Abel in 1826 [1]. Note that for z=0z=0, (3.2.12) reduces to the binomial theorem. Riordan [64, pp. 18–27] gives a comprehensive account of Abel’s identity and its generalizations, though he does not use Lagrange inversion.

3.3. Fuss-Catalan numbers

The Fuss-Catalan (or Fuß-Catalan) numbers of order pp (also called generalized Catalan numbers) are the numbers 1p​n+1​(p​n+1n)=1(p−1)​n+1​(p​nn)\frac{1}{pn+1}\binom{pn+1}{n}=\frac{1}{(p-1)n+1}\binom{pn}{n}, which reduce to Catalan numbers for p=2p=2. They were first studied by N. Fuss in 1791 [21]. As we shall see, they are the coefficients of the power series cp​(x)c_{p}(x), satisfying the functional equation

cp​(x)=1+x​cp​(x)p,c_{p}(x)=1+xc_{p}(x)^{p}, (3.3.1)

or equivalently,

cp​(x)=11−x​cp​(x)p−1,c_{p}(x)=\frac{1}{1-xc_{p}(x)^{p-1}},

as was shown using Lagrange inversion by Liouville [49].

An account of these generating functions can be found Graham, Knuth, and Patashnik [32, pp. 200–204].

It follows easily from (3.3.1) that

cp​(x)−1=x​cp​(x)p=(x(1+x)p)⟨−1⟩,\displaystyle c_{p}(x)-1=xc_{p}(x)^{p}=\left(\frac{x}{(1+x)^{p}}\right)^{\langle-1\rangle}, (3.3.2)
x​cp​(x)p−1=(x​(1−x)p−1)⟨−1⟩,\displaystyle xc_{p}(x)^{p-1}=\bigl(x(1-x)^{p-1}\bigr)^{\langle-1\rangle},
x​cp​(xp−1)=(x−xp)⟨−1⟩,\displaystyle xc_{p}(x^{p-1})=(x-x^{p})^{\langle-1\rangle},

and

cp′​(x)=cp​(x)p1−p​x​cp​(x)p−1.c^{\prime}_{p}(x)=\frac{c_{p}(x)^{p}}{1-pxc_{p}(x)^{p-1}}.

Lagrange inversion gives

cp​(x)k=∑n=0∞kp​n+k​(p​n+kn)​xnc_{p}(x)^{k}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{pn+k}\binom{pn+k}{n}x^{n} (3.3.3)

for all kk. With R⁡(t)=1+x​tpR(t)=1+xt^{p} we have R′​(t)=p​x​tp−1R^{\prime}(t)=pxt^{p-1} so

1−R′​(cp​(x))=1−p​x​cp​(x)p−1=1−p⁡(cp​(x)−1)/cp​(x)=1−p+p​cp​(x)−1,1-R^{\prime}(c_{p}(x))=1-pxc_{p}(x)^{p-1}=1-p(c_{p}(x)-1)/c_{p}(x)=1-p+pc_{p}(x)^{-1},

and thus by (2.4.6),

∑n=0∞(p​n+kn)​xn=cp​(x)k1−p​x​cp​(x)p−1=cp​(x)k+11−(p−1)​(cp​(x)−1).\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{pn+k}{n}x^{n}=\frac{c_{p}(x)^{k}}{1-pxc_{p}(x)^{p-1}}=\frac{c_{p}(x)^{k+1}}{1-(p-1)(c_{p}(x)-1)}. (3.3.4)

Equivalently,

∑n=0∞(p​n+kn)​(x(1+x)p)n=(1+x)k+11−(p−1)​x\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{pn+k}{n}\left(\frac{x}{(1+x)^{p}}\right)^{n}=\frac{(1+x)^{k+1}}{1-(p-1)x}

and

∑n=0∞(p​n+kn)(x(1−x)p−1)n=1(1−p​x)​(1−x)k.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{pn+k}{n}\bigl(x(1-x)^{p-1}\bigl)^{n}=\frac{1}{(1-px)(1-x)^{k}}.

The convolution identities obtained from (3.3.3) and (3.3.4), known as Rothe-Hagen identities [65, 33, 30] are

∑i+j=nkp​i+k​(p​i+ki)⋅lp​j+l​(p​j+lj)=k+lp​n+k+l​(p​n+k+ln).\sum_{i+j=n}\frac{k}{pi+k}\binom{pi+k}{i}\cdot\frac{l}{pj+l}\binom{pj+l}{j}=\frac{k+l}{pn+k+l}\binom{pn+k+l}{n}.

and

∑i+j=nkp​i+k​(p​i+ki)​(p​j+lj)=(p​n+k+ln).\sum_{i+j=n}\frac{k}{pi+k}\binom{pi+k}{i}\binom{pj+l}{j}=\binom{pn+k+l}{n}.

Next, we prove Jensen’s formula [39]

∑l=0n(j+p​ll)​(r−p​ln−l)=∑i=0n(j+r−in−i)​pi.\sum_{l=0}^{n}\binom{j+pl}{l}\binom{r-pl}{n-l}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{j+r-i}{n-i}p^{i}. (3.3.5)

By (3.3.4) we have

∑l=0∞(p​l+jl)​xl​∑m=0∞(p​m+km)​xm\displaystyle\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}\binom{pl+j}{l}x^{l}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\binom{pm+k}{m}x^{m} =cp​(x)j+k(1−p​x​cp​(x)p−1)2\displaystyle=\frac{c_{p}(x)^{j+k}}{(1-pxc_{p}(x)^{p-1})^{2}}
=cp​(x)j+k1−p​x​cp​(x)p−1​∑i=0∞pi​xi​cp​(x)(p−1)​i\displaystyle=\frac{c_{p}(x)^{j+k}}{1-pxc_{p}(x)^{p-1}}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}p^{i}x^{i}c_{p}(x)^{(p-1)i}
=∑i=0∞pi​xi​cp​(x)j+k+(p−1)​i1−p​x​cp​(x)p−1\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{p^{i}x^{i}c_{p}(x)^{j+k+(p-1)i}}{1-pxc_{p}(x)^{p-1}}
=∑i=0∞pi​xi​∑m=0∞(p​m+j+k+(p−1)​im)​xm\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}p^{i}x^{i}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\binom{pm+j+k+(p-1)i}{m}x^{m}
=∑n=0∞xn​∑i=0n(p​n+j+k−in−i)​pi.\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{pn+j+k-i}{n-i}p^{i}.

Equating coefficients of xnx^{n} on both sides gives

∑l=0n(p​l+jl)​(p⁡(n−l)+kn−l)=∑i=0n(p​n+j+k−in−i)​pi.\sum_{l=0}^{n}\binom{pl+j}{l}\binom{p(n-l)+k}{n-l}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{pn+j+k-i}{n-i}p^{i}.

Setting k=r−p​nk=r-pn gives (3.3.5).

We also have analogues of Theorems 3.2.1 and 3.2.5 for Fuss-Catalan numbers.

Theorem 3.3.7.

Let ii and jj be nonnegative integers with i<ji<j. Then

∑n=0∞(p​n+i)!n!​((p−1)​n+j)!​xn(1+x)p​n+i+1\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(pn+i)!}{n!\,((p-1)n+j)!}\frac{x^{n}}{(1+x)^{pn+i+1}}

is a polynomial ui,j​(x)u_{i,j}(x) in xx of degree j−i−1j-i-1.

Proof.

We have

∑n=0∞(p​n+i)!n!​((p−1)​n+j)!\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(pn+i)!}{n!\,((p-1)n+j)!} xn(1+x)p​n+i+1\displaystyle\frac{x^{n}}{(1+x)^{pn+i+1}}
=∑n=0∞(p​n+i)!n!​((p−1)​n+j)!​xn​∑l=0∞(−1)l​(p​n+i+ll)​xl\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(pn+i)!}{n!\,((p-1)n+j)!}x^{n}\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{l}\binom{pn+i+l}{l}x^{l}
=∑m=0∞xm​∑n=0m(p​n+i)!n!​((p−1)​n+j)!​(−1)m−n​((p−1)​n+i+mm−n).\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}x^{m}\sum_{n=0}^{m}\frac{(pn+i)!}{n!\,((p-1)n+j)!}(-1)^{m-n}\binom{(p-1)n+i+m}{m-n}.

For m≥j−im\geq j-i, the coefficient of xmx^{m} may be rearranged to

(m−(j−i))!m!​∑n=0m(−1)m−n​(mn)​((p−1)​n+i+mm−(j−i)).\frac{\bigl(m-(j-i)\bigr)!}{m!}\sum_{n=0}^{m}(-1)^{m-n}\binom{m}{n}\binom{(p-1)n+i+m}{m-(j-i)}.

The sum is the mmth difference of a polynomial of degree less than mm and is therefore 0. For m=j−i−1m=j-i-1, the coefficient of xj−i−1x^{j-i-1} reduces to

1m!​∑n=0m(−1)m−n​(mn)​1(p−1)​n+j,\frac{1}{m!}\sum_{n=0}^{m}(-1)^{m-n}\binom{m}{n}\frac{1}{(p-1)n+j},

which is nonzero by the well-known identity

∑n=0m(−1)n​(mn)​an+a=(m+aa)−1,\sum_{n=0}^{m}(-1)^{n}\binom{m}{n}\frac{a}{n+a}=\binom{m+a}{a}^{-1},

so the degree of the polynomial is not less than j−i−1j-i-1. ∎

The first few values of these polynomials are

ui,i+1​(x)\displaystyle u_{i,i+1}(x) =1i+1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{i+1}
ui,i+2​(x)\displaystyle u_{i,i+2}(x) =1(i+1)​(i+2)−p−1(i+2)​(p+i+1)​x\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(i+1)(i+2)}-\frac{p-1}{(i+2)(p+i+1)}x
ui,i+3​(x)\displaystyle u_{i,i+3}(x) =1(i+1)​(i+2)​(i+3)−(p−1)​(p+2​i+4)(i+2)​(i+3)​(p+i+1)​(p+i+2)​x\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(i+1)(i+2)(i+3)}-\frac{(p-1)(p+2i+4)}{(i+2)(i+3)(p+i+1)(p+i+2)}x
+(p−1)2(i+3)​(p+i+2)​(2​p+i+1)​x2\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt+\frac{(p-1)^{2}}{(i+3)(p+i+2)(2p+i+1)}x^{2}

As a simple example of Theorem 3.3.7, the number of 2-stack-sortable permutations of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\} is

an=2​(3​n)!(n+1)!​(2​n+1)!=4​(3​n)!n!​(2​n+2)!a_{n}=2\frac{(3n)!}{(n+1)!\,(2n+1)!}=4\frac{(3n)!}{n!\,(2n+2)!}

(see [57, Sequence A000139]), so by Theorem 3.3.7, with p=3p=3, i=0i=0, and j=2j=2, ∑n=0∞an​xn/(1+x)3​n+1\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}{x^{n}}/(1+x)^{3n+1} is a polynomial of degree 1, which is easily computed to be 2−x2-x. Then by (3.3.2), we find that

∑n=0∞an​xn=3​c3​(x)−c3​(x)2,\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}x^{n}=3c_{3}(x)-c_{3}(x)^{2},

which can be checked directly from (3.3.3).

There is a result similar to Theorem 3.3.7 for i≥ji\geq j, which we state without proof.

Theorem 3.3.8.

Let ii and jj be nonnegative integers with i≥ji\geq j. Then

(1−(p−1)​x)2​(i−j)+1​∑n=0∞(p​n+i)!n!​((p−1)​n+j)!​xn(1+x)p​n+i+1(1-(p-1)x)^{2(i-j)+1}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(pn+i)!}{n!\,((p-1)n+j)!}\frac{x^{n}}{(1+x)^{pn+i+1}}

is a polynomial in xx of degree at most i−ji-j. ∎

Exercise 3.3.9.

Prove Theorem 3.3.8.

3.4. Narayana and Fuss-Narayana numbers

The Narayana numbers may be defined by N⁡(n,i)=1n​(ni)​(ni−1)N(n,i)=\frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{i}\binom{n}{i-1} for n≥1n\geq 1. They have many combinatorial interpretations, in terms of Dyck paths, ordered trees, binary trees, and noncrossing partitions.

It is not hard to see from the formula for Narayana numbers that N⁡(n,i)=N⁡(n,n+1−i)N(n,i)=N(n,n+1-i). A generating function for the Narayana that exhibits this symmetry is given by the solution to the equation

f=(1+x​f)​(1+y​f).f=(1+xf)(1+yf). (3.4.1)

Lagrange inversion gives

fk\displaystyle f^{k} =∑n=0∞kn​[tn−k]⁡(1+x​t)n​(1+y​t)n\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}(1+xt)^{n}(1+yt)^{n}
=∑n=0∞kn​[tn−k]⁡∑i,j(ni)​(nj)​xi​yj​ti+j\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}\sum_{i,j}\binom{n}{i}\binom{n}{j}x^{i}y^{j}t^{i+j}
=∑i,j=0∞ki+j+k​(i+j+ki)​(i+j+kj)​xi​yj.\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=0}^{\infty}\frac{k}{i+j+k}\binom{i+j+k}{i}\binom{i+j+k}{j}x^{i}y^{j}.

In particular

f\displaystyle f =∑i,j=0∞1i+j+1​(i+j+1i)​(i+j+1i+1)​xi​yj\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{i+j+1}\binom{i+j+1}{i}\binom{i+j+1}{i+1}x^{i}y^{j}
=∑n=1∞∑i=0n−1N⁡(n,i+1)​xi​yn−i−1.\displaystyle=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}N(n,i+1)x^{i}y^{n-i-1}.

Equation (3.4.1) can be solved explicitly to give

f=1−x−y−(1−x−y)2−4​x​y2​x​y.f=\frac{1-x-y-\sqrt{(1-x-y)^{2}-4xy}}{2xy}.
Exercise 3.4.1.

Prove that

(1+x​f)r​(1+y​f)s(1−x−y)2−4​x​y=∑i,j(r+i+ji)​(s+i+jj)​xi​yj\frac{(1+xf)^{r}(1+yf)^{s}}{\sqrt{(1-x-y)^{2}-4xy}}=\sum_{i,j}\binom{r+i+j}{i}\binom{s+i+j}{j}x^{i}y^{j}

and

(1+x​f)r​(1+y​f)s\displaystyle(1+xf)^{r}(1+yf)^{s} =∑i,j[(r+i+j−1i)​(s+i+jj)−(r+i+ji)​(s+i+j−1j−1)]​xi​yj\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\left[\binom{r+i+j-1}{i}\binom{s+i+j}{j}-\binom{r+i+j}{i}\binom{s+i+j-1}{j-1}\right]x^{i}y^{j}
=∑i,jr​s+r​i+s​j(r+i+j)​(s+i+j)​(r+i+ji)​(s+i+jj)​xi​yj.\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\frac{rs+ri+sj}{(r+i+j)(s+i+j)}\binom{r+i+j}{i}\binom{s+i+j}{j}x^{i}y^{j}.

The first formula is equivalent to a well-known generating function for Jacobi polynomials; see Carlitz [8].

We may generalize (3.4.1) to

f=(1+x1f)r1(1+x2f)r2⋯(1+xmf)rm,f=(1+x_{1}f)^{r_{1}}(1+x_{2}f)^{r_{2}}\cdots(1+x_{m}f)^{r_{m}}, (3.4.2)

for which Lagrange inversion gives

fk=∑n=k∞∑i1+⋯+im=n−kkn(r1​ni1)⋯(rm​nim)x1i1⋯xmim.f^{k}=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\sum_{i_{1}+\cdots+i_{m}=n-k}\frac{k}{n}\binom{r_{1}n}{i_{1}}\cdots\binom{r_{m}n}{i_{m}}x_{1}^{i_{1}}\cdots x_{m}^{i_{m}}. (3.4.3)

These numbers reduce to Catalan numbers for k=m=1,r1=2k=m=1,r_{1}=2 and to Narayana numbers for k=1,m=2,r1=r2=1k=1,m=2,r_{1}=r_{2}=1. For k=1,m=2,r1=1k=1,m=2,r_{1}=1 they are sometimes called Fuss-Narayana numbers; see Armstrong [3], Cigler [15], Edelman [19], Eu and Fu [20], and Wang [75]. The numbers for k=1k=1, ri=1r_{i}=1 for all ii have been called generalized Fuss-Narayana numbers by Lenczewski and Sałapata [48]; they have also been studied by Edelman [19], Stanley [69], and Xu [78]. The case k=1,m=3,r2=−r1,r3=1k=1,m=3,r_{2}=-r_{1},r_{3}=1 of these numbers was considered by Krattenthaler, [44, equation (31)]. We note that if r1=⋯=rmr_{1}=\cdots=r_{m}, then ff is a symmetric function of x1,…,xmx_{1},\dots,x_{m}, and this symmetric function arises in the study of algebraic aspects of parking functions [69].

If we set ri=−sir_{i}=-s_{i} in (3.4.2) and replace xix_{i} with −xi-x_{i}, and ff with gg, then (3.4.2) becomes

g=1(1−x1g)s1(1−x2g)s2⋯(1−xmg)sm,g=\frac{1}{(1-x_{1}g)^{s_{1}}(1-x_{2}g)^{s_{2}}\cdots(1-x_{m}g)^{s_{m}}}, (3.4.4)

and, with the formula (−ai)=(−1)i​(a+i−1i)\binom{-a}{i}=(-1)^{i}\binom{a+i-1}{i}, (3.4.3) becomes

gk=∑n=k∞∑i1+⋯+im=n−kkn(s1​n+i1−1i1)⋯(sm​n+im−1im)x1i1⋯xmim.g^{k}=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\sum_{i_{1}+\cdots+i_{m}=n-k}\frac{k}{n}\binom{s_{1}n+i_{1}-1}{i_{1}}\cdots\binom{s_{m}n+i_{m}-1}{i_{m}}x_{1}^{i_{1}}\cdots x_{m}^{i_{m}}. (3.4.5)

These numbers reduce to Catalan numbers for k=m=s1=1k=m=s_{1}=1. For s1=⋯=sm=1s_{1}=\cdots=s_{m}=1 they have been considered by Aval [4] and (for k=1k=1) by Stanley [69].

Of special interest are the cases of (3.4.2) that reduce to a quadratic equation, since in these cases there are simple explicit formulas for ff. If we take m=1m=1, r1=r2=1r_{1}=r_{2}=1, and r3=−1r_{3}=-1 then with a change of variable names and one sign we have

f=(1+x​f)​(1+y​f)1−z​f,f=\frac{(1+xf)(1+yf)}{1-zf},

with the solution

f=1−x−y−(1−x−y)2−4​x​y−4​z2​(x​y+z),f=\frac{1-x-y-\sqrt{(1-x-y)^{2}-4xy-4z}}{2(xy+z)},

and (3.4.3) gives

fk=∑n=k∞∑i1+i2+i3=n−kkn​(ni1)​(ni2)​(n+i3−1i3)​xi1​yi2​zi3.f^{k}=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}=n-k}\frac{k}{n}\binom{n}{i_{1}}\binom{n}{i_{2}}\binom{n+i_{3}-1}{i_{3}}x^{i_{1}}y^{i_{2}}z^{i_{3}}.

Another case of (3.4.2) that reduces to a quadratic is f=(1+x​f)​(1+y​f)f=\sqrt{(1+xf)(1+yf)}; we leave the details to the reader.

3.5. Raney’s equation

G. Raney [62] considered the equation

f=∑m=1∞Am​eBm​f,f=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}A_{m}e^{B_{m}f}, (3.5.1)

in which ff is a power series in the indeterminates AmA_{m} and BmB_{m}. He used Prüfer’s correspondence to give a combinatorial derivation of a formula for the coefficients in this power series.

We can use Lagrange inversion to give a formula for the coefficients of ff.

Theorem 3.5.1.

Let ff be the power series in AmA_{m} and BmB_{m} satisfying (3.5.1), and let kk be a positive integer. Let i1,i2,…i_{1},i_{2},\dots and j1,j2,…j_{1},j_{2},\dots be nonnegative integers, only finitely many of which are nonzero. If i1+i2+⋯=k+j1+j2+⋯i_{1}+i_{2}+\dots=k+j_{1}+j_{2}+\cdots then the coefficient of A1i1A2i2⋯B1j1B2j2⋯A_{1}^{i_{1}}A_{2}^{i_{2}}\cdots B_{1}^{j_{1}}B_{2}^{j_{2}}\cdots in fkf^{k} is

k(i1+i2+⋯−1)!i1!i2!⋯i1j1j1!i2j2j2!⋯k\frac{(i_{1}+i_{2}+\cdots-1)!}{i_{1}!\,i_{2}!\cdots}\frac{i_{1}^{j_{1}}}{j_{1}!}\frac{i_{2}^{j_{2}}}{j_{2}!}\cdots

and if i1+i2+⋯≠k+j1+j2+⋯i_{1}+i_{2}+\dots\neq k+j_{1}+j_{2}+\cdots then the coefficient is zero.

Proof.

Applying equation (2.4.3) to (3.5.1) gives

fk\displaystyle f^{k} =∑n=k∞kn​[tn−k]⁡(∑mAm​eBm​t)n\displaystyle=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}\biggl(\sum_{m}A_{m}e^{B_{m}t}\biggr)^{n}
=∑n=k∞kn[tn−k]∑i1+i2+⋯=nn!i1!i2!⋯A1i1A2i2⋯ei1​B1​tei2​B2​t⋯\displaystyle=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+\cdots=n}\frac{n!}{i_{1}!\,i_{2}!\cdots}A_{1}^{i_{1}}A_{2}^{i_{2}}\cdots e^{i_{1}B_{1}t}e^{i_{2}B_{2}t}\cdots
=∑n=k∞kn[tn−k]∑i1+i2+⋯=nn!i1!i2!⋯A1i1A2i2⋯∑j1(i1​B1​t)j1j1!∑j2(i2​B2​t)j2j2!⋯\displaystyle=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+\cdots=n}\frac{n!}{i_{1}!\,i_{2}!\cdots}A_{1}^{i_{1}}A_{2}^{i_{2}}\cdots\sum_{j_{1}}\frac{(i_{1}B_{1}t)^{j_{1}}}{j_{1}!}\sum_{j_{2}}\frac{(i_{2}B_{2}t)^{j_{2}}}{j_{2}!}\cdots
=∑n=k∞∑i1+i2+⋯=nj1+j2+⋯=n−kk(n−1)!i1!i2!⋯A1i1A2i2⋯B1j1B2j2⋯i1j1j1!i2j2j2!⋯,\displaystyle=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i_{1}+i_{2}+\cdots=n\\ j_{1}+j_{2}+\cdots=n-k\end{subarray}}k\frac{(n-1)!}{i_{1}!\,i_{2}!\cdots}A_{1}^{i_{1}}A_{2}^{i_{2}}\cdots B_{1}^{j_{1}}B_{2}^{j_{2}}\cdots\frac{i_{1}^{j_{1}}}{j_{1}!}\frac{i_{2}^{j_{2}}}{j_{2}!}\cdots,

and the formula follows. ∎

A combinatorial derivation of Raney’s formula has also been given by D. Knuth [42, Section 2.3.4.4].

4. Proofs

In this section we give several proofs of the Lagrange inversion formula.

4.1. Residues

The simplest proof of Lagrange inversion is due to Jacobi [38]. We define the residue res⁡f⁡(x)\res f(x) of a Laurent series f⁡(x)=∑nfn​xnf(x)=\sum_{n}f_{n}x^{n} to be f−1f_{-1}.

Jacobi proved the following change of variables formula for residues:

Theorem 4.1.1.

Let ff be a Laurent series and let g⁡(x)=∑n=1∞gn​xng(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}g_{n}x^{n} be a power series with g1≠0g_{1}\neq 0. Then

res⁡f⁡(x)=res⁡f⁡(g⁡(x))​g′​(x).\res f(x)=\res f(g(x))g^{\prime}(x).
Proof.

By linearity, it is sufficient to prove the formula when f⁡(x)=xkf(x)=x^{k} for some integer kk. If k≠−1k\neq-1 then res⁡xk=0\res x^{k}=0 and

res⁡g​(x)k​g′​(x)=res⁡dd​x​g​(x)k+1/(k+1)=0,\res g(x)^{k}g^{\prime}(x)=\res\frac{d\ }{dx}g(x)^{k+1}/(k+1)=0,

since the residue of a derivative is 0.

If k=−1k=-1 then res⁡xk=1\res x^{k}=1 and

res⁡g​(x)k​g′​(x)\displaystyle\res g(x)^{k}g^{\prime}(x) =res⁡g′​(x)/g⁡(x)=res⁡g1+2​g2​x+⋯g1​x+g2​x2+⋯\displaystyle=\res g^{\prime}(x)/g(x)=\res\frac{g_{1}+2g_{2}x+\cdots}{g_{1}x+g_{2}x^{2}+\cdots}
=res⁡1x⋅g1+2​g2​x+⋯g1+g2​x+⋯=1.∎\displaystyle=\res\frac{1}{x}\cdot\frac{g_{1}+2g_{2}x+\cdots}{g_{1}+g_{2}x+\cdots}=1.\qed

Jacobi’s paper [38] contains a multivariable generalization of Theorem 4.1.1; see also Gessel [28] and Xin [77].

Now let f⁡(x)f(x) and g⁡(x)g(x) be compositional inverses. Then for any Laurent series ϕ\phi,

[xn]⁡ϕ⁡(f)=res⁡ϕ⁡(f)xn+1=res⁡ϕ⁡(f⁡(g))​g′gn+1=res⁡ϕ⁡(x)​g′gn+1.\mathop{[x^{n}]}\phi(f)=\res\frac{\phi(f)}{x^{n+1}}=\res\frac{\phi(f(g))g^{\prime}}{g^{n+1}}=\res\frac{\phi(x)g^{\prime}}{g^{n+1}}.

This is equation (2.1.7), which we have already seen is equivalent to the other forms of Lagrange inversion.

Exercise 4.1.2.

Let ff be a Laurent series and let g⁡(x)=∑n=m∞gn​xng(x)=\sum_{n=m}^{\infty}g_{n}x^{n} be a Laurent series with gm≠0g_{m}\neq 0. Show that if f⁡(g⁡(x))f(g(x)) is well-defined as a Laurent series then

m​res⁡f=res⁡f⁡(g⁡(x))​g′​(x).m\res f=\res f(g(x))g^{\prime}(x).
Exercise 4.1.3.

(Hirzebruch [34]; see also Kneezel [41].) Use the change of variables formula (Theorem 4.1.1) to show that the unique power series f⁡(x)f(x) satisfying

res⁡(f⁡(x)x)n=1\res\left(\frac{f(x)}{x}\right)^{n}=1

for all n≥1n\geq 1 is f⁡(x)=x/(1−e−x)f(x)=x/(1-e^{-x}).

4.2. Induction

In this proof and the next we consider the equation f=x​R​(f)f=xR(f), where R⁡(t)R(t) is a power series. If R⁡(t)R(t) has no constant term then f=0f=0 and the formulas are trivial. So we may assume that R⁡(t)R(t) has a nonzero constant term, and thus ff exists and is unique, since it is the compositional inverse of x/R⁡(x)x/R(x).

We now give an inductive proof of (2.1.2): for any power series ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t),

[xn]⁡ϕ⁡(f)=[tn]⁡(1−t​R′​(t)R⁡(t))​ϕ​(t)​R​(t)n.\mathop{[x^{n}]}\phi(f)=\mathop{[t^{n}]}\left(1-\frac{tR^{\prime}(t)}{R(t)}\right)\phi(t)R(t)^{n}. (4.2.1)

(As noted in section 2, this implies that (4.2.1) holds more generally when ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) is a Laurent series.)

We first take care of the case in which ϕ⁡(t)=1\phi(t)=1. The case ϕ⁡(t)=1\phi(t)=1, n=0n=0 is trivial. If ϕ⁡(t)=1\phi(t)=1 and n>0n>0, we have

(1−t​R′​(t)R⁡(t))​R​(t)n\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{tR^{\prime}(t)}{R(t)}\right)R(t)^{n} =R​(t)n−t​R′​(t)​R​(t)n−1\displaystyle=R(t)^{n}-tR^{\prime}(t)R(t)^{n-1}
=R​(t)n−tn​dd​t​R​(t)n.\displaystyle=R(t)^{n}-\frac{t}{n}\frac{d\ }{dt}R(t)^{n}. (4.2.2)

Now for any power series u⁡(t)u(t),

[tn]⁡(u⁡(t)−tn​u′​(t))=0.\mathop{[t^{n}]}\left(u(t)-\frac{t}{n}u^{\prime}(t)\right)=0.

With(4.2.2), this proves (4.2.1) for ϕ⁡(t)=1\phi(t)=1, n>0n>0.

Now we prove the formula (4.2.1) by induction on nn. It is clear that (4.2.1)holds for n=0n=0. Now let us suppose that for some nonnegative integer mm, (4.2.1) holds for all ϕ\phi when n=mn=m. We now want to show that (4.2.1) holds for all ϕ\phi when n=m+1n=m+1. By linearity and the case ϕ⁡(t)=1\phi(t)=1, it is enough to prove (4.2.1) for n=m+1n=m+1 and ϕ⁡(t)=tk\phi(t)=t^{k}, where k≥1k\geq 1. In this case we have

[xm+1]⁡fk\displaystyle\mathop{[x^{m+1}]}f^{k} =[xm+1]⁡fk−1⋅x​R​(f)\displaystyle=\mathop{[x^{m+1}]}f^{k-1}\cdot xR(f)
=[xm]⁡fk−1​R​(f)\displaystyle=\mathop{[x^{m}]}f^{k-1}R(f)
=[tm]⁡(1−t​R′​(t)R⁡(t))​tk−1​R​(t)​R​(t)m\displaystyle=\mathop{[t^{m}]}\left(1-\frac{tR^{\prime}(t)}{R(t)}\right)t^{k-1}R(t)R(t)^{m}
=[tm+1]⁡(1−t​R′​(t)R⁡(t))​tk​R​(t)m+1.\displaystyle=\mathop{[t^{m+1}]}\left(1-\frac{tR^{\prime}(t)}{R(t)}\right)t^{k}R(t)^{m+1}.

4.3. Factorization

Another proof is based on a version of the “factor theorem”: if f=x​R​(f)f=xR(f) then t−ft-f divides t−x​R​(t)t-xR(t). This proof is taken from Gessel [27] but it is similar to Lagrange’s original proof [47].

We will prove (2.2.1), which gives a formula for fkf^{k} where f=f⁡(x)f=f(x) satisfies f=x​R​(f)f=xR(f).

First we recall Taylor’s theorem for power series: if P⁡(t)P(t) is a power series in tt, and α\alpha is an element of the coefficient ring, then

P⁡(t)=∑n=0∞(t−α)nn!​P(n)​(α),P(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(t-\alpha)^{n}}{n!}P^{(n)}(\alpha), (4.3.1)

as long as this sum is summable. (The case P⁡(t)=tmP(t)=t^{m} of (4.3.1) is just the binomial theorem, and the general case follows by linearity.)

Now let us apply (4.3.1) with P⁡(t)=t−x​R​(t)P(t)=t-xR(t) and α=f\alpha=f, where f=x​R​(f)f=xR(f) so that P⁡(f)=0P(f)=0. Then we have

t−x​R​(t)\displaystyle t-xR(t) =0+(t−f)​(1−x​R′​(f))+(t−f)2​S​(x,t)\displaystyle=0+(t-f)\bigl(1-xR^{\prime}(f)\bigr)+(t-f)^{2}S(x,t)
=(t−f)​Q​(x,t),\displaystyle=(t-f)Q(x,t), (4.3.2)

where S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) is a power series and Q⁡(x,t)Q(x,t) is a power series with constant term 1.

Equation (4.3.2) is an identity in the ring C⁡[[x,t]]C[[x,t]], which is naturally embedded in the ring C​((t))​[[x]]C((t))[[x]] of power series in xx with coefficients that are Laurent series in tt. In this ring, series like ∑n=0∞(x/t)n\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(x/t)^{n} are allowed, even though they have infinitely many negative powers of tt, since the coefficient of any power of xx is a Laurent series in tt. We now do some computations in C​((t))​[[x]]C((t))[[x]].

By (4.3.2), we have 1−x​R​(t)/t=(1−f/t)​Q​(x,t).1-xR(t)/t=(1-f/t)Q(x,t). Since x​R​(t)/txR(t)/t and f/tf/t are divisible by xx and Q⁡(x,t)Q(x,t) is a power series in xx and tt with constant term 1, we may take logarithms to obtain

−log⁡(1−x​R​(t)/t)=−log⁡(1−f/t)−log⁡Q⁡(x,t).-\log(1-xR(t)/t)=-\log(1-f/t)-\log Q(x,t). (4.3.3)

Note that log⁡Q⁡(x,t)\log Q(x,t) is a power series in xx and tt, and so has no negative powers of tt. Now we equate coefficients of xn​t−kx^{n}t^{-k} on both sides of (4.3.3) where nn and kk are both positive integers. On the left we have [t−k]⁡(R⁡(t)/t)n/n=[tn−k]⁡R​(t)n/n\mathop{[t^{-k}]}(R(t)/t)^{n}/n=\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}R(t)^{n}/n and on the right we have [xn]⁡fk/k.\mathop{[x^{n}]}f^{k}/k. Thus,

[xn]⁡fk=kn​[tn−k]⁡R​(t)n,\mathop{[x^{n}]}f^{k}=\frac{k}{n}\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}R(t)^{n},

which is (2.2.1).

Exercise 4.3.1.

(Gessel [27].) Derive (2.2.2) similarly.

4.4. Combinatorial proofs

There are several different combinatorial proofs of Lagrange inversion. They all interpret the solution ff of f=x​R​(f)f=xR(f) or f=R⁡(f)f=R(f) as counting certain trees. Here ff may be interpreted as either an ordinary or exponential generating function and thus different types of trees may be involved.

In ordinary generating function proofs, ff will count unlabeled ordered trees (also called plane trees), which are rooted trees in which the children of each vertex are linearly ordered. (See Figure 1.)

More generally, fkf^{k} will count kk-tuples of ordered trees, which we also call forests of ordered trees.

If f=x​R​(f)f=xR(f), where R⁡(t)=∑i=0∞ri​tiR(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}r_{i}t^{i}, then the coefficient of xnx^{n} in ff is the sum of the weights of the ordered trees with a total of nn vertices, where the weight of a tree is the product of the weights of its vertices and the weight of a vertex with ii children is rir_{i}. (For example, the tree of Figure 1 has weight r03​r22r_{0}^{3}r_{2}^{2}.) So to give a combinatorial proof of formula (2.2.1), we show that the sum of the weights of all kk-tuples of ordered trees with a total of nn vertices is (k/n)​[tn−k]⁡R​(t)n(k/n)\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}R(t)^{n}, or equivalently by (2.5.1), the number of kk-tuples of ordered trees in which nin_{i} vertices have ii children for each ii is equal to

kn​(nn0,n1,n2,…)\frac{k}{n}\binom{n}{n_{0},n_{1},n_{2},\dots} (4.4.1)

if

n=∑kniandn−k=∑ki​ni,n=\sum_{k}n_{i}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002ptn-k=\sum_{k}in_{i}, (4.4.2)

and is zero otherwise. W. T. Tutte [74] gave the case k=1k=1 of (4.4.1), which he derived (in a roundabout way) from Lagrange inversion.

We can also work with exponential generating functions. One way to do this is to consider the equation f=x​∑i=0∞si​fi/i!f=x\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}s_{i}f^{i}\!/i! where xx is the exponential variable and the sns_{n} are weights. Then by the properties of exponential generating functions (see, e.g., [70, Chapter 5]) ff counts labeled rooted trees where a vertex with ii children is weighted sis_{i}. More precisely, the coefficient of xn/n!x^{n}\!/n! in fk/k!f^{k}/k! is the sum of the weights of all forests of kk rooted trees with vertex set [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}. Then Lagrange inversion in the form (2.5.1) is equivalent to assertion that the number of forests of kk rooted trees with vertex set [n][n] in which nin_{i} vertices have ii children is equal to

(n−1)!(k−1)! 0!n01!n12!n2⋯​(nn0,n1,…)\frac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!\,0!^{n_{0}}1!^{n_{1}}2!^{n_{2}}\cdots}\binom{n}{n_{0},n_{1},\dots} (4.4.3)

with the same conditions on n0,n1,…n_{0},n_{1},\dots as before. (See Stanley [70, p. 30, Corollary 5.3.5].)

Another exponential generating function approach is to consider the equation

f=∑i=0∞si​fii!f=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}s_{i}\frac{f^{i}}{i!}

where we work with exponential generating functions in the variables s0,s1,…s_{0},s_{1},\dots. Then by the properties of multivariable exponential generating functions, the coefficient of

s0n0n0!​s1n1n1!​…\frac{s_{0}^{n_{0}}}{n_{0}!}\frac{s_{1}^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}!}\dots

in fk/k!f^{k}/k! is the number of forests of kk rooted trees in which for each ii, nin_{i} vertices have ii children and these vertices are labeled 1,2,…,ni1,2,\dots,n_{i}. (Since vertices with the same label have different numbers of children, there are no nontrivial label-preserving automorphisms of these forests.) For example, such a forest with k=2k=2, n0=5n_{0}=5, n2=3n_{2}=3, and ni=0n_{i}=0 for i∉{0,2}i\notin\{0,2\} is show in Figure 2.

Then Lagrange inversion in the form (2.5.1) (with x=1x=1) is equivalent to the assertion that the number of such forests is

(n−1)!(k−1)! 0!n01!n12!n2⋯,\frac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!\,0!^{n_{0}}1!^{n_{1}}2!^{n_{2}}}\cdots, (4.4.4)

where n=n0+n1+⋯n=n_{0}+n_{1}+\cdots and n1+2​n2+3​n3+⋯=n−kn_{1}+2n_{2}+3n_{3}+\cdots=n-k.

4.5. Raney’s proof

The earliest combinatorial proof of Lagrange inversion is that of Raney [61]. We sketch here a proof that is based on Raney’s though the details are different. (See also Stanley [70, pp. 31–35 and 39–40].) We define the suffix code c⁡(T)c(T) for an ordered tree TT to be a sequence of nonnegative integers defined recursively: If the root rr of TT has jj children, and the trees rooted at the children of rr are T1,…,TjT_{1},\dots,T_{j}, then c⁡(T)c(T) is the concatenation c(T1)⋯c(Tj)jc(T_{1})\cdots c(T_{j})j. More generally, the suffix code for a kk-tuple (T1,…,Tk)(T_{1},\dots,T_{k}) of ordered trees is the concatenation c(T1)⋯c(Tk)c(T_{1})\cdots c(T_{k}). We defined the reduced code of a tree or kk-tuple of trees to be the sequence obtained from the suffix code by subtracting 1 from each entry.

For example the suffix code of the kk-tuple of trees in Figure 3 is 0 0 2 0 10\,0\,2\,0\,1 and the reduced code is 1¯​1¯​ 1​1¯​ 0\bar{1}\,\bar{1}\,1\,\bar{1}\,0, where 1¯\bar{1} denotes −1-1.

The following lemma can be proved by induction:

Lemma 4.5.1.
  1. (i)

    A forest of ordered trees is uniquely determined by its reduced code.

  2. (ii)

    A sequence a1a2⋯ana_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n} of integers greater than or equal to −1-1 is the reduced code of an ordered kk-forest if and only if a1+⋯+an=−ka_{1}+\cdots+a_{n}=-k and a1+⋯+aia_{1}+\cdots+a_{i} is negative for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. ∎

We also need a lemma, due to Raney, that generalizes the “cycle lemma” of Dvoretzky and Motzkin [18]. It can be proved by induction, or in other ways. (See, e.g., Stanley [70, pp. 32–33].)

Lemma 4.5.2.

Let a1⋯ana_{1}\cdots a_{n} be a sequence of integers greater than or equal to −1-1 with sum −k<0-k<0. Then there are exactly kk integers ii, with 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, such that the sequence ai⋯ana1⋯ai−1a_{i}\cdots a_{n}a_{1}\cdots a_{i-1} has all partial sums negative. ∎

We can now prove Lagrange inversion. We want to prove that the sum of the weights of all kk-forests with nn vertices is k/nk/n times

[tn−k]⁡R​(t)n=[t−k]⁡(R⁡(t)t)n,\mathop{[t^{n-k}]}R(t)^{n}=\mathop{[t^{-k}]}\left(\frac{R(t)}{t}\right)^{n},

where R⁡(t)=∑n=0∞sn​tnR(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}s_{n}t^{n}. Let us define the weight of a sequence a1⋯ana_{1}\cdots a_{n} of integers to be the product sa1+1⋯san+1s_{a_{1}+1}\cdots s_{a_{n}+1}. Then by Lemma 4.5.1, the sum of the weights of all kk-forests with nn vertices is the sum of the weights of all sequences of integers of length nn, with entries greater than or equal to −1-1, with sum −k-k, and with all partial sums negative. It is clear that [t−k]⁡(R⁡(t)/t)n\mathop{[t^{-k}]}(R(t)/t)^{n} is the sum of the weights of all sequences of integers of length nn, with entries greater than or equal to −1-1, and with sum −k-k. But by Lemma 4.5.2, a proportion k/nk/n of these sequences have all partial sums negative.

4.6. Proofs by labeled trees

We can derive Lagrange inversion by counting labeled trees with the following result, which seems to have first been proved by Moon [52].

Theorem 4.6.1.

Let mm be a positive integer and let d1,d2,…,dmd_{1},d_{2},\dots,d_{m} be positive integers. Then the number of (unrooted) trees with vertex set [m][m] in which vertex ii has degree did_{i} is the multinomial coefficient

(m−2d1−1,…,dm−1)\binom{m-2}{d_{1}-1,\dots,d_{m}-1} (4.6.1)

if ∑i=1mdi=2​(m−1)\sum_{i=1}^{m}d_{i}=2(m-1) and is 0 otherwise.

We will prove Theorem 4.6.1 a little later; we first look at some of its consequences. A corollary of Theorem 4.6.1 allows us to count forests of rooted trees:

Corollary 4.6.2.

Let e1,e2,…,ene_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{n} be nonnegative integers with e1+e2+⋯+en=n−ke_{1}+e_{2}+\cdots+e_{n}=n-k, and let kk be a positive integer. Then the number of forests of kk rooted trees, with vertex set [n][n], in which vertex ii has eie_{i} children is

(n−1k−1,e1,…​en).\binom{n-1}{k-1,e_{1},\dots e_{n}}.
Proof.

Let TT be a tree on [n+1][n+1] in which vertex n+1n+1 has degree kk, and vertex ii has degree ei+1e_{i}+1 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n (so that ∑i=1nei=n−k\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{i}=n-k). Removing vertex n+1n+1 from TT and rooting the resulting component trees at the neighbors of n+1n+1 in TT gives a forest FF of kk rooted trees in which vertex ii has eie_{i} children, and this operation gives a bijection from trees on [n+1][n+1] in which vertex n+1n+1 has degree kk and vertex ii has degree ei+1e_{i}+1 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n to the set of rooted forests of kk trees on [n][n] in which vertex ii has eie_{i} children. The result then follows from Lemma 4.6.1. ∎

It follows from Corollary 4.6.2 that the number of forests of kk rooted trees in which for each ii, nin_{i} vertices have ii children and these vertices are labeled 1,2,…,ni1,2,\dots,n_{i} is given by (4.4.4), which as we saw earlier, is equivalent to Lagrange inversion.

Now to count kk-forests on [n][n] in which nin_{i} vertices have ii children, we first assign the number of children to each element of [n][n], which can be done in (nn0,n1,…)\binom{n}{n_{0},n_{1},\dots} ways. For each assignment, the number of trees is

(n−1)!(k−1)! 0!n01!n1⋯\frac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!\,0!^{n_{0}}1!^{n_{1}}\cdots}

Multiplying these factors gives (4.4.3).

We now present sketches of three proofs of Theorem 4.6.1. They all depend on the fact that a tree with at least two vertices must have at least one leaf (vertex of degree 1).

The first proof uses Prüfer’s correspondence [60]. Given a tree T1T_{1} with vertex set [n][n], let a1a_{1} be the least leaf of T1T_{1} and let b1b_{1} be the unique neighbor of a1a_{1} in T1T_{1}. Let T2T_{2} be the result of removing a1a_{1} and its incident edge from T1T_{1}. Let a2a_{2} be the least leaf of T2T_{2} and let b2b_{2} be its neighbor in T2T_{2}. Continue in this way to define b3,⋯,bn−2b_{3},\cdots,b_{n-2}. Then the Prüfer code of T1T_{1} is the sequence (b1,b2,⋯,bn−2)(b_{1},b_{2},\cdots,b_{n-2}). It can be shown that the map that takes a tree to its Prüfer code is a bijection from the set of trees with vertex set [n][n], for n≥2n\geq 2, to the set of sequences b1​b2​…​bn−2b_{1}b_{2}\dots b_{n-2} of elements of [n][n], with the property that a vertex of degree dd appears d−1d-1 times in the Prüfer code. Then, as noted by Moon [52], Theorem 4.6.1 is an immediate consequence, since the multinomial coefficient counts Prüfer codes of trees in which vertex ii has degree did_{i}.

The second proof is by induction, and is due to Moon [53] (see also [54, p. 13]). For m≥2m\geq 2, let T⁡(m,d1,…,dm)T(m;d_{1},\dots,d_{m}) be the number of trees on [m][m] in which vertex ii has degree did_{i} and let U⁡(m,d1​…,dm)U(m;d_{1}\dots,d_{m}) be the multinomial coefficient (4.6.1), which is 0 if any did_{i} is less than 1 or if ∑idi≠2​(n−1)\sum_{i}d_{i}\neq 2(n-1).

Clearly T⁡(m,d1,…,dm)T(m;d_{1},\dots,d_{m}) is equal to U⁡(m,d1​…,dm)U(m;d_{1}\dots,d_{m}) for m=2m=2. Now suppose that n>2n>2 and that T⁡(m,d1,…,dm)T(m;d_{1},\dots,d_{m}) is equal to U⁡(m,d1​…,dm)U(m;d_{1}\dots,d_{m}) for m=n−1m=n-1 and all choices of d1,…,dmd_{1},\dots,d_{m}.

We next observe that if dn=1d_{n}=1 then

T⁡(n,d1,…,dn)=∑i=1n−1T⁡(n−1,d1,…,di−1,…,dn−1)T(n;d_{1},\dots,d_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}T(n-1;d_{1},\dots,d_{i}-1,\dots,d_{n-1}) (4.6.2)

since every tree in which nn is a leaf is obtained by joining vertex nn with an edge to some vertex of a tree on [n−1][n-1], increasing by 1 the degree of this edge and leaving the other degrees unchanged. Then by the inductive hypothesis and a well-known recurrence for multinomial coefficients, T⁡(n,d1,…,dn)T(n;d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) is equal to U⁡(n,d1​…,dn)U(n;d_{1}\dots,d_{n}). We have assumed that dn=1d_{n}=1, but since T⁡(n,d1,…,dn)T(n;d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) is symmetric in d1,…,dnd_{1},\dots,d_{n} and every tree has at least one leaf, the result holds without this assumption.

Rényi [63] (see also Moon [54, p. 13]) gave an elegant variation of this proof. He showed by induction that for m≥2m\geq 2 the number of trees on [m][m] with degree sequence (d1,…,dm)(d_{1},\dots,d_{m}), i.e., trees in which vertex ii has degree did_{i}, is the coefficient of x1d1−1⋯xmdm−1x_{1}^{d_{1}-1}\cdots x_{m}^{d_{m}-1} in (x1+⋯+xm)m−2(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{m})^{m-2}. The result clearly holds for m=2m=2, so suppose that n>2n>2 and that the result holds when m=n−1m=n-1. To show that it holds for m=nm=n, we note that every tree on [n][n] has at least one leaf, so by symmetry, we may assume, without loss of generality, that dn=1d_{n}=1. Thus we need only show that the number of trees on [n][n] with degree sequence (d1,…,dn−1,1)(d_{1},\dots,d_{n-1},1) is the coefficient of x1d1−1⋯xn−1dn−1−1x_{1}^{d_{1}-1}\cdots x_{n-1}^{d_{n-1}-1} in

(x1+⋯+xn−1)n−2=(x1+⋯+xn−1)⋅(x1+⋯+xn−1)n−3.(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n-1})^{n-2}=(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n-1})\cdot(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n-1})^{n-3}.

But every tree on [n][n] in which vertex nn is a leaf is obtained by joining vertex nn with an edge to some vertex of a tree on [n−1][n-1], increasing by 1 the degree of this vertex and leaving the other degrees unchanged. Thus by the induction hypothesis, the contribution from trees in which vertex nn is joined to vertex ii is xi​(x1+⋯+xn−1)n−3x_{i}(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n-1})^{n-3} and the result follows.
